And remember the Friend of God in the slaughter of his son, when his Creator said, and when they both submitted."

So then: if the hearts themselves are in the flood, the apparatus of beliefs and principles has been ruined, and from its ruin arises the ruin of the movement of life and the deviation of conduct. The heart has been given this importance because it is the workshop of the blood and the source of the fluid of life. If it is corrupted, it must seep into the rest of the limbs, and they too become corrupted; and if the heart is sound, its soundness must seep into all the limbs so that they become sound, as in the noble hadith:

"Verily, in the body there is a piece of flesh: if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Verily, it is the heart." (3)

Then He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And they have deeds other than that which they are doing.﴾ (23:63) [al-Mu'minun]: meaning the matter does not stop with them at the question of beliefs; rather they have many other deeds into which they will fall. The Truth, glory be to Him, mentions to them only the peaks of transgressions and samples of them, but in His knowledge, may He be exalted, and in the Preserved Tablet, it is recorded that they will do this and do that, even if they themselves do not know that this will happen from them. But their Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, knows by the freedom of power what was and what will be.

Among the wonders of God's power is that He judges His disbelieving servant that he will do such and such, yet none of the disbelievers opposes it by saying: "God has judged me to such and such, but I will not do it," so that God's judgment about him would be untrue. For the Truth, glory be to Him, does not dictate only what He makes flow upon us, but also the choice of the servant and his intention, although the servant is free to act or not to act.

This matter is clear in His saying concerning Abu Lahab: ﴿Ruined are the hands of Abu Lahab, and ruined is he. His wealth did not avail him, nor what he earned. He will burn in a fire of blazing flame.﴾ (111:1-3) [al-Masad]. His saying: ﴿He will burn..(3)﴾ [al-Masad] indicates the future; the Truth, glory be to Him, judged that he would be in the Fire. Abu Lahab was among a community and gathering of disbelieving people, and among them some believed. So who guarantees that Abu Lahab would hear this judgment and yet not believe and die a disbeliever?

Moreover, was it not possible for this "heedless one" to stand before the assembly and say: "There is no god but God, and Muhammad is the Messenger of God," and enter Islam, so that the judgment concerning him would be untrue? But this is the speech of God and His eternal decree, which is not reversed, and no one opposes it, whatever his affair is in his hand while he is able to choose. This is from the freedom of God's power in His action and over His creatures in their actions.

So the meaning of: ﴿they have deeds..(63)﴾ [al-Mu'minun] is a judgment that is not reversed or denied, even if its subject is informed of it, because the knowledge of God, may He be exalted, comprehends what was and what will be. It is as if the Truth, glory be to Him, is saying: the freedom of power is not only in what I do, but in what others do, to whom I have given freedom of choice.

1 - Talla: he threw him down on his face on the ground. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/101].
2 - From the poetry of the Shaykh, may God be pleased with him.
3 - Agreed upon. Related by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (52), and likewise Muslim in his Sahih (1599), from the hadith of al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, may God be pleased with him.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66)) on surah 23, verse 64:

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿Until, when We seize their affluent ones with punishment, behold, they cry out for help.﴾ (23:64)

Meaning: after they had associated partners with Allah and disbelieved in Him, and after their hearts had become immersed in heedlessness and blindness, when some punishment touches them they cry out and shriek. And who can bear even a blast or a whiff of the punishment of Allah?

As for the meaning of ﴿We seize…﴾ (23:64) [al-Mu'minun]: the word al-akhdh (seizing) has a wide scope in the Book of Allah. Al-akhdh is the forceful taking-hold of something that its owner does not wish to be taken from him, and it suggests violence and severity, such that the one seized cannot escape however much he tries.

From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿A seizing of One Mighty, Omnipotent﴾ (54:42) [al-Qamar]: meaning a severe seizing from which one writhes and cannot break free.

And His saying: ﴿And the cry seized those who did wrong…﴾ (11:67) [Hud].

And He says: ﴿Indeed, His seizing is painful and severe﴾ (11:102) [Hud].

As for the meaning of ﴿their affluent ones…﴾ (23:64) [al-Mu'minun]: from al-itraf (affluence), which is luxury and comfort. Life rests on necessities that sustain life and luxuries that make it happy, graceful and enriched. So the affluent man is one who has blessings beyond necessities. It is said: taraffa al-rajul yatarraf (the man became affluent), from the pattern of faraha yafrahu (to rejoice); and atrafathu al-ni'mah means the blessing made him insolent; and Allah atrafahu means He widened the blessing upon him and increased him in it. The greater the affluence, the more painful and the more severe the seizing.

We have already mentioned the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of…﴾ (6:44) [al-An'am]: meaning, of the method of Allah. We did not constrict upon them; rather: ﴿We opened upon them the gates of everything, until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly, and at once they were in despair. So the last remnant of the people who did wrong was cut off…﴾ (6:44–45) [al-An'am]. Here the blow is more intense and the grief greater.

The discussion here concerns the disbelievers of Quraysh. How did Allah seize them while they were in affluence, when all the bounties of the Arabian Peninsula were poured out upon them until they lived a life of luxury and comfort?

Allah seized them in the midst of their affluence with drought and years of famine. Therefore, when the Prophet (ﷺ) saw them grown affluent and insolent through the blessing, he said: "O Allah, tighten Your grip upon Mudar, and make it upon them years like the years of Joseph." (1)

Allah, exalted is He, answered the supplication of His Prophet, so drought and famine struck them until they ate carrion and al-'ilhiz (2), which is the hair of the slaughtered animal or its wool mixed with its blood after it dried and congealed under the heat of the sun. This is what is meant by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Until, when We seize their affluent ones with punishment…﴾ (23:64).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿behold, they cry out for help﴾ (23:64): they shriek and wail. Thus Abu Sufyan, after they had eaten carrion and refuse, said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "O Muhammad, are you not a mercy to the worlds? Then supplicate Allah to relieve us." So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) supplicated his Lord until He relieved them. (3)

Or: what is meant by the punishment here is what befell them on the day of Badr, when Allah humbled them: some of them were killed, some were taken captive, their lordship collapsed and their prestige was lost. They had been tormenting and killing the believers, placing them in the heat of the sun and putting large stones upon their bellies, until Allah, exalted is He, sent down in that harsh state which the believers were suffering: ﴿The multitude will be routed and will turn their backs﴾ (54:45) [al-Qamar].

They received the verse with astonishment, to the point that 'Umar said: "What multitude is this that will be routed? There was no sign at all of the believers' victory." Then when the day of Badr came and the believers saw what had befallen the disbelievers, 'Umar himself said: "Allah has spoken truly: the multitude will be routed, and it has been routed."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿behold, they cry out for help﴾ (23:64): yaj'aru means he cries out with a loud voice. A person does not cry out except when he is in a trial whose causes he cannot repel, so he cries out seeking one who will rescue him, and he raises his voice so that everyone around him hears, as they say: (yaj'aru).

Al-ju'ar is like al-khuwar, meaning they bellow like calves, after they had been men, lords and tyrants. "Why did you not remain lords? Why do you cry out now?" In the time of hardship it was expected of them to hold firm and to show fortitude, so that the slaves and the poor who believed would not gloat over them, as the poet says: (4)

"And show the gloaters my fortitude, that I
am not humbled by the calamities of time." (5)

But, far-fetched! The punishment has befallen them, and they cannot deceive themselves now. There is nothing left for them but crying out, seeking by it a rescuer and one who saves them from ruin.

1 - From Abu Hurayrah: the Prophet (ﷺ), when he raised his head from the last rak'ah, would say: "O Allah, tighten Your grip upon Mudar. O Allah, make it years like the years of Joseph." Narrated by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (1006) and Ahmad in his Musnad (2/470, 502, 521).
2 - Al-'ilhiz: dried blood which is pounded with camel hair in times of famine and eaten. Ibn Shumayl said:
"And if the hospitality of Qahtan is a filth and an 'ilhiz, then how base it is — woe to you, what a deed!"
3 - From Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Abu Sufyan came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Muhammad, I adjure you by Allah and by the ties of kinship, for we have eaten the 'ilhiz — meaning the hair and the blood." Then Allah revealed: ﴿And We had seized them with punishment, yet they did not humble themselves before their Lord, nor do they supplicate﴾ (23:76) [al-Mu'minun]. Cited by Ibn Kathir in his tafsir (3/251), attributing it to Ibn Abi Hatim.
4 - The poet is Abu Dhu'ayb, Khuwaylid ibn Khalid al-Hudhali (died 27 AH).
5 - Al-tadha'da'): submission and abasement. In a hadith: "No man humbles himself (yatada'da'a) before another seeking worldly gain except that two-thirds of his religion departs," meaning he submits and abases himself. Al-tajallud: displaying endurance, which is patience and steadfastness. [Lisan al-'Arab, entries: d-'-'  and j-l-d]

Then the Almighty says:

﴿Do not cry out for help today; indeed, you will not be helped by Us.﴾ (23:65)

The Almighty responds to them: ﴿Do not cry out for help today...﴾ (23:65), because the one who cries out (yajʼaru) calls upon someone who will help him, and you will not be helped. ﴿Indeed, you will not be helped by Us...﴾ (23:65): you will not be helped from Our side. For I help My friends, I help My messengers, and I help whoever helps Me. So cut off any expectation of My help for you, for it is I who sent down upon you what caused you to cry out, so how would I remove it from you?

In another place, the Almighty speaks of the disbelievers who colluded against Him, and who encouraged one another to be bold against the Qur'an and against the Prophet (ﷺ), and who applauded whoever plunged into speaking against them both: ﴿Assemble those who did wrong, and their spouses (wa-azwājahum),(1) and what they used to worship, apart from Allah, and guide them to the path of Hellfire. And stop them, for they are to be questioned. What is the matter with you that you do not help one another? Nay, today they are submitting.﴾ (37:22–26)

So: do not cry out, for you will not be helped by Us. How could We help you with this crying out of yours, when you have turned away from My signs?

(1) Al-Nu'man ibn Bashir said: "By their spouses (azwājahum) is meant their likes and their counterparts." And ʻUmar ibn al-Khattab said: "The companions of adultery will come with the companions of adultery, the companions of usury with the companions of usury, and the companions of intoxicants with the companions of intoxicants." [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 4/4].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 23, verse 66:

﴿Indeed My verses were recited to you, but you turned back on your heels,﴾

How can you call upon Allah for help and cry out to Him, when His verses are recited to you, explaining to you and establishing for you the existence of Allah through the cosmic signs, establishing for you the truthfulness of the Messenger through the miracles, and conveying to you the method of Allah in the verses that carry the rulings? Yet you have become blind to all of that.

As for the meaning of ﴿you turned back on your heels﴾ [al-Mu'minun]: the 'aqib (heel) is the back part of the foot. Instead of walking forward as Allah created him, and as He made for him lights by which he sees the path and is guided to the place of his feet, he walks backward on his heels, as if they had been seized by something that reversed the direction of his movement. Why? Because they became blind to the causes of guidance, so they stumble about in the labyrinths of life without guidance, like one who walks with his back turned, not knowing where his feet are. And this is what they did to themselves.

In driving, this backward movement is called (marshadir, i.e. reverse gear), and a person in it needs someone to direct him and guide his movement to the right or left, because he cannot see.

The meaning, then, is: do not blame anyone but yourself, for you deprived yourself of the causes of guidance. After it came to you and was placed before you, you shut your eyes to it.

In another place, concerning Satan, He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿And when the two hosts came in sight, he turned back on his heels and said, "Indeed, I am free of you..."﴾ [al-Anfal: 48].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 23, verse 67:

﴿Boasting thereof, telling tales by night, speaking evil.﴾ (67)

Root: k-b-r (kibr). With a kasra on the ba' (kibar), it denotes age: one says "kabura fulan" meaning he was young and then grew old. With a damma on the ba' (kubr), it denotes an abstract and lofty thing, as in His saying ﴿It is a grave word that comes out of their mouths..﴾ (5) [al-Kahf]: meaning, it is great.

The meaning of istikbar (ist-ikbar) is to seek and pursue greatness, as istifham means to seek understanding, whereas in reality one is not great in himself; he is in need of others. The one who is great in himself is the one who possesses in himself the foundations of life, its necessities and its comforts, and draws them from no one.

But a human being's necessities of life and the causes of his comfort are bestowed upon him by others, so it is not proper for him to be arrogant. Whoever wishes to be arrogant, let him be arrogant with something intrinsic to himself, such as health, wealth, or authority, etc. But all of these are things bestowed upon you: the healthy may become sick, and the wealthy may become poor.

Therefore, majesty belongs to God alone, for He is the Giver to others and the One who bestows upon creation that by which they could be proud. Among the attributes of His majesty and perfection, glorified is He, is (al-Mutakabbir), because He, glorified is He, is the Lord of all creation. It is in the interest of creation that the one who is greatly exalted be God alone, so that no one raises his head over His creatures and domineers over them.

Thus does the Truth, glorified is He, protect His creatures from one another. If your Lord were to act arrogantly toward you and decree upon you a decree, because you did something while you are one person, know that He is arrogant toward all others, who are many, should they do this to you. Thus the attribute of majesty belongs to Almighty God for your benefit.

For an example of this, and to God belongs the highest likeness: it is in the interest of a family that it have only one elder to whom it returns, and among the sayings of the common people is (whoever has no elder, let him buy himself an elder), because he is the balance by which affairs are set right and the rudder by which the life of the household is steered.

We have said that among His names, exalted is He, is (al-Kabir), and we do not say (al-Akbar), even though it is a form of intensification. Why? Because akbar is an intensive form among us human beings: we say "this is great and that is greater," "this is strong and that is stronger." This is not said of His attributes, exalted is He, for if you said "God is akbar," the meaning would be that you have associated another with Him, for He is greater and others are great. Therefore "Allahu akbar" is said only in the call to prayer.

So then: the mustakbir is the one who seeks the qualifications of greatness while having none of those qualifications intrinsic to his own self. A human being should not be arrogant unless he possesses the intrinsic elements of greatness, and the created being possesses none of that.

As for ﴿Boasting thereof..﴾ (67) [al-Mu'minun]: the hā' in (bihi) is an ambiguous pronoun, whose referent identifies it, as when you say: "A man came to me, so I honored him." What removed the ambiguity of the hā' is its referent, a man. In the verse, no noun preceded to which the pronoun returns, but the discourse here is about the Messenger who was sent to them, and the Qur'an revealed to them as a miracle and a method. Therefore the pronoun returns only to one of these two.

Or: the pronoun in (bihi) returns to the Sacred House of God, which was the cause of the standing and status of Quraysh among the Arabs, and gave them a position of lordship and honor, so that they traveled on trading journeys to Yemen and to Syria without anyone attacking them, at a time when plunder, looting, raiding and highway robbery had spread among the tribes.

This standing would not have been theirs had it not been for the Sacred House of God, which the Arabs visit every year, and whose service and custodianship were in the hands of Quraysh. Therefore they boasted by it over the whole community. Not only that, but they also dared to act insolently toward the House itself.

Then He, exalted is He, says: ﴿telling tales by night..﴾ (67) [al-Mu'minun]: (al-samar) is a group who converse at night. They used to gather around the House of God at night, speaking against the Prophet (ﷺ), reviling him and engaging in talk against him, and against the Qur'an that was revealed to him.(1)

Would that they had been talking at the House about goodness, but rather it was with (hujr), and (hujr) is the foul speech about Muhammad (ﷺ) and the Qur'an.

The matter of these people is astonishing: how do they do this while they are in the courtyard of the House of God, which granted them lordship and standing? How do they engage in talk against the Messenger of God, who came to cleanse this House from idols and their filth? It is a breach of manners toward God, toward His Messenger, and toward the Qur'an, of which the poet's words are true:

"I taught him archery every day, / but when his arm grew strong, he shot me. / How many times I taught him the composition of verses, / but when he composed a verse, he satirized me."

These people boasted over the whole community by means of the House, yet they did not preserve its sanctity; they made it a place for night talk, for abuse, for folly and frivolity, and for everything unbecoming to it. For them the Qur'an is "tales of the ancients," and Muhammad is for them a sorcerer, a soothsayer, a poet, and a madman... and so on.

And the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, reminds you of the necessities of your life as a gift from Him, glorified is He, and a bounty. When Abraha came to demolish this ancient House and transfer this greatness and sanctity to Abyssinia, you had no power to repel him nor ability to protect the House. Had he demolished it, your dignity and lordship among the tribes would have been lost, and they would have dared against you as they dared against others. But God protected His House and defended its sanctities, so much so that the elephant itself understood this lesson, and stood in its place, not moving toward the House in particular; when they directed it to any other direction, it would walk.

It is related that one of them(2) said to the elephant, addressing it: "Kneel, Mahmud, and return in peace," meaning: save your skin, for you are in the land of the Sacred God. And as the poet said(3):

"The elephant was held at al-Mughammas until it / came to crawl as if hamstrung."(4)

Thus God turned them back humiliated and repelled, and preserved the House for you, and maintained your lordship.

So notice the transition from Surah al-Fil to Surah Quraysh. He, exalted is He, says: ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant? Did He not make their plot into misguidance? And He sent against them birds in flocks, striking them with stones of hard clay, and made them like eaten straw.﴾ [al-Fil] (1-5): meaning, like chaff and crumbs that the winds scatter.

Then He says at the beginning of Quraysh: ﴿For the accustomed security of the Quraysh﴾ (1) [Quraysh]: meaning, what befell the companions of the elephant. The lam in (li-ilaf) is the lam of cause: what befell the companions of the elephant happened so that Quraysh would be accustomed to the journey of winter and summer ﴿their accustomed journey in winter and summer﴾ (2) [Quraysh]. Since God, exalted is He, has protected you and protected the House for you and preserved your lordship, it was incumbent upon you to worship Him alone without partner: ﴿So let them worship the Lord of this House (3) who fed them against hunger and secured them against fear﴾ (4) [Quraysh].

1 - Said by Abdullah ibn Abbas and others, as transmitted from him by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir (6/4671).
2 - From Aisha, may God be pleased with her, who said: "I saw the leader of the elephant and its driver, both blind and crippled, begging for food in Mecca." Recorded by al-Bayhaqi in (Dala'il al-Nubuwwah) "1/125." Its editor said: the report is in the Sira of Ibn Hisham (1/59), where it reads "begging from the people." It is also transmitted by al-Hafiz Ibn Kathir in al-Bidaya wa'l-Nihaya (2/174).
3 - He is: Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt ibn Abi Rabi'a.
4 - Al-Mughammas: a place near Mecca. Al-ma'qur: the slaughtered, i.e., as if they had cut one of its legs and then slaughtered it; it is used of camels. [Lisan al-Arab, root: '-q-r]

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 23, verse 68:

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿Have they not pondered the Word? Or has there come to them what had not come to their fathers, the earliest ones?﴾ (68)

In this verse and the verses after it, He—glorified and exalted is He—intends to rebuke them for several matters, one after another.

The first of them: ﴿Have they not pondered the Word?﴾ (23:68). The interrogative here is for rebuke and reproach: What has happened to these people? Have they not understood the Word that came to them in the Qur'an, when they are the people of eloquence, rhetoric and clear expression, the people of speech in all its arts, to the point that they held fairs and markets for it and hung it on the wall?

Therefore it is not reasonable that you would not understand the Qur'an, when it has come to you in a style at a higher level of rhetoric and eloquence. You must have understood it and grasped what is in it, as evidenced by your saying: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a man of importance from the two towns?﴾ (43:31).

Thus the liar is betrayed by his own nature, and his speech reveals what is in his heart. So your objection is not to the Qur'an but to Muhammad, because he is a poor man from among the average people. The matter, then, is a dispute over leadership and temporal authority. But did these people not realize that Muhammad (ﷺ) did not come to strip them of their authority, or to rise above them, but came to govern them by the method of God, and bore harm, fatigue and hardship for the sake of their comfort and happiness?

The Prophet (ﷺ) came to take up judgment and carry the method of God as a burden, not as an honour. This is evidenced by the fact that he lived at a standard lower than yours. You do not see the Messenger of God except as the least of them in food and drink, the least of them in clothing and furnishings. Even his relatives were poor, and yet he forbade them the zakat, which he permitted for the general Muslim poor. Likewise, people inherit from him while he does not inherit from them.

And after all that you say: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a man of importance from the two towns?﴾ (43:31). It appears that you have become accustomed to servitude to the great and the tyrants, to servitude to other than God, and it has been hard for you that God should free you from this servitude through the hand of a humble, poor man from among you, who came to reform you and bring you out of servitude to the created to servitude to the Creator, mighty and majestic is He.

Did not one of the heads of disbelief say about the Qur'an: "By God, its upper part bears fruit, its lower part is abundant, it is high and nothing is higher than it" (1).

So: ﴿Have they not pondered the Word?﴾ (23:68) is a rebuke, because they did understand the Qur'an, but they envied Muhammad (ﷺ) that it should be sent down to him and that he should attain this station over them, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Or do they envy the people for what God has given them of His bounty?﴾ (4:54).

The second matter: ﴿Or has there come to them what had not come to their fathers, the earliest ones?﴾ (23:68). That is: there has come to them a strange matter they have no precedent for, namely that a messenger should come from God. Yet this matter is familiar to them: among their forefathers were Abraham (peace be upon him) and Ishmael, and they believed in both of them. So this is not a strange issue; rather they know it well. But what prevented them in the first case prevents them in this one: it is envy of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Therefore He, exalted is He, says: ﴿And if you asked them who created them, they would surely say, "God."﴾ (43:87).

1 - This saying was uttered by al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, transmitted by Ibn Hisham in al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (1/270). The reason was that the nobles of Quraysh gathered to agree on one opinion regarding the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ). Al-Walid rejected everything the people said about Muhammad until he uttered this saying, then said: "You will not say anything about this except that it will be known to be false. The closest statement you can make about it is that he is a sorcerer, who brought a speech that is sorcery, by which he separates a man from his father, from his brother, from his wife, and from his clan."

The third matter: ﴿Or do they not recognize their Messenger, so that they deny him?﴾ (23:69).

That is, is it that a messenger has come down to them from heaven whose conduct, character, lineage and way of life before he was sent they do not know? Indeed they know him well. Before his mission they called him "the Truthful, the Trustworthy" (al-Sadiq al-Amin), they accepted his judgment among them in the matter of the Black Stone, they entrusted him with their deposits and their precious wealth, and they never caught him in a lie, a betrayal, or any of the lapses of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic period).

This matter was explained in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves...﴾ (9:128). That is: from your own kind, your own species, your own tribe. He is not a stranger to you; his conduct, his way of life and his character are known to you. If you never found him lying to people, could you imagine that he would lie against the Creator?

Did the Messenger of Allah, at the very beginning of his mission, when he informed people that he was the Messenger of Allah, bring the Qur'an to compel people to believe in him? No. Rather, it came to challenge those who did not believe. As for those who believed from the start: as soon as Muhammad said, "I am the Messenger of Allah," they said, "You have spoken the truth." The basis for their affirmation was what they had tested of him in the past, what they knew of his truthfulness, and that he had never lied at all. Therefore the standard among the Companions was that the Messenger of Allah had spoken; if he said it, the matter was settled, because he was truthful and none of them doubted his truthfulness.

Accordingly, when Abu Bakr said, regarding the matter of the Night Journey and the Ascension (al-Isra' wa'l-Mi'raj): "If he said it, then he has spoken the truth," the Prophet (ﷺ) accepted it out of regard for Abu Bakr and said: "Abu Bakr and I were in the Jahiliyyah like two horses racing (kafarasay rahan)," meaning in good character and upright conduct: "I preceded him to prophethood, so he followed me; and had he preceded me, I would have followed him."

When Jibril (peace be upon him) came down to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at the beginning of the revelation and overwhelmed him, he went to Lady Khadijah (may Allah be pleased with her) and related to her what had happened to him, as though seeking her understanding of it. He did not tell her that he was a messenger from Allah. Nevertheless, she took him to Waraqa ibn Nawfal, who had knowledge of the earlier scriptures. When Waraqa ibn Nawfal heard what had happened, he said: "This is the Namus (the angel of revelation) that was sent down to Musa. Would that I were alive when your people drive you out." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Will they drive me out?" He said: "No man has ever brought the like of what you have brought except that he was opposed. If your day reaches me, I shall support you with a mighty support." (3)

Yet the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) remained fearful and anxious that this might be something from the Shaytan. Lady Khadijah reassured him, for this is not conceivable concerning the Messenger of Allah. She said to him: "Indeed you join the ties of kinship, you bear the burdens of the weak (takassib al-ma'dum), you bear the burdens of the destitute (tahmil al-kall), you help in the calamities of time, and by Allah, Allah will never let you down." (6)

From here they regarded Lady Khadijah as the first mujtahida in Islam, because she exercised independent reasoning and inferred, from the Messenger of Allah's conduct before the mission, evidence of his truthfulness after the mission. Therefore she was the first to be called Umm al-Mu'minin (Mother of the Believers). Some of the knowers said: "Khadijah was a mother of the believers, including the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)", because at that stage of his life he needed a mother more than he needed a young bride to pamper him. Lady Khadijah (may Allah be pleased with her) indeed played the role of a mother to the Messenger of Allah: she embraced him, reassured him, and stood beside him in the most difficult and distressing times.

We also observe in the verse ﴿Or do they not recognize their Messenger...﴾ (23:69) that the Messenger is attributed to them: "rasuluhum", meaning "their messenger". As for the attribution to Allah the Exalted, "Rasul Allah" (Messenger of Allah), the meaning is "a messenger from Him." Thus the meaning varies with the variation of the attribution.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 23, verse 70:

﴿Or do they say, "There is madness in him"? Rather, he has brought them the truth, but most of them are averse to the truth.﴾ (23:70):

The fourth point concerns God's rebuke of them: ﴿Or do they say, "There is madness in him"...﴾ [al-Mu'minun] (70). That is, jinn (madness). Madness means that the rational faculty, which weighs actions according to benefit and harm, ceases to function, so that a person does beneficial good and abandons harmful evil. Let us consider: which trait of madness is to be found in Muhammad (ﷺ)?

Set aside the question of religion and the Deity, and take his character instead. Character is something on which everyone agrees and which they praise, even if they themselves are the opposite of it. The liar loves the truthful, and acknowledges that truthfulness is nobility and honour; the miser loves the generous, and the quick-tempered loves the forbearing. Do you not see that the liar practises his lying upon people, yet does not love the one who lies to him?

Do you not see that the false witness saves another by his testimony, and yet falls in the eyes of that person and is despised by him? So much so that the people of wisdom say: the false witness raises your head over the adversary by his testimony, while your foot tramples on his dignity; and whoever makes you a place of disgrace has fallen from his sight, even if you assist him in his affair.

Therefore, the measures of character are one. So measure Muhammad by his character, not by the religion and message he brought. Look at his character among you, and not one of you will be able to accuse him of anything in his character. And since he is not accused in his character, he is likewise not accused in his intellect, for intellect is the balance of character and its foundation.

Therefore his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, says concerning him:

{Nun. By the pen and what they inscribe. You are not, by the grace of your Lord, a madman. And indeed for you is a reward never cut off. And indeed, you are of a great moral character.} (al-Qalam 68:1-4). Your great character is the greatest proof that you are not mad.

Therefore Muhammad is free of this accusation, and the whole matter is as the Exalted says: ﴿Rather, he has brought them the truth...﴾ [al-Mu'minun] (70). This is his fault in their view, because the truth enrages the people of falsehood who profit from it. Some see the truth in the good that comes to them, but if it is in something from which they do not benefit, they consider it evil. Therefore, if you wish to judge a trait, judge it when it is against you, not when it is for you. For example, you should dislike the liar whether he lies to you or lies about you. Therefore, take matters as being both for you and against you.

When the Exalted, glory be to Him, restricts your gaze toward the forbidden things of others, do not chafe or say, "He has deprived me of the pleasure of looking," and so on. Rather, look at how He has restricted your eyes while you are one person, and restricted the eyes of others from your forbidden things while they are many.

Then the Exalted says: ﴿And most of them are averse to the truth﴾ [al-Mu'minun] (70). It is natural that the people of falsehood, whose oppression and tyranny have spread, should dislike the truth that came to balance the scales and to straighten the crooked in the movement of life. The people of falsehood's dislike of the Messenger of Allah ought to have been a criterion for affirming him, not denying him. We should say: as long as the people of falsehood dislike this, it must be that he is upon the truth, otherwise they would not dislike it.

1 - "Ghayr mamnun": that is, not cut off, i.e., everlasting. It may also mean not spoiled by reminding of favours, reproach, and boasting about it. The two meanings do not conflict. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/240].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 23, verse 71:

﴿And if the truth had followed their desires, the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them would have been corrupted. Rather, We have brought them their reminder, but they, from their reminder, are turning away.﴾ (23:71):

So then: affairs do not run according to the desire of the created being, but according to the wishes of the Creator, because the Creator, glory be to Him, is the maker of this universe, and every maker is jealous of his creation. This is witnessed even in the craftsmanship of human beings, and you may imagine what would happen if someone spoiled what he had made.

The justice of things is that they run in accordance with the wishes of the Maker, not the desire of the made, because desires are controlled by other things. If a person moved in the course of his life according to his desire, he would take what is not his, accept bribery, and incline toward immorality and deviation, because he apparently sees that he benefits from this and does not look to the consequence and the final outcome. He has looked at a fleeting, time-limited pleasure and forgotten a heavy burden he will not be able to bear afterwards.

Therefore the Truth, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And if the truth had followed their desires, the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them would have been corrupted..﴾ (23:71). You may say: Yes, following desires corrupts the earth and corrupts the movement of life in it, but how would it corrupt the heaven? And does anyone have power over it?

We say: Was it not among the wishes of these people: ﴿And they said, "We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth. (90) Or you have a garden of palm trees and grapes and cause rivers to gush forth within it in force. (91) Or you cause the sky to fall upon us in fragments, as you have claimed..﴾ (17:90-92).

So then: among their desires is that the sky should collapse, even upon their heads. And what corruption is beyond this? Likewise, if you followed their desires, the heavens and the earth would be corrupted, and not only this, but ﴿and whoever is in them..﴾ (23:71), since their corruption would extend to encompass everything in existence.

Therefore the Prophet (ﷺ) restricts these desires in his saying: "None of you truly believes until his desire is subject to what I have brought." Because he (ﷺ) ﴿does not speak from desire. (3) It is not but a revelation revealed.﴾ (53:3-4).

Some orientalists have objected, stopping at this verse: ﴿nor does he speak from desire (3)﴾ (53:3). They say: this means that all his speech is correct, so why would his Lord amend some rulings for him? And that would mean that the amended ruling, when he uttered it, was spoken from desire.

Had these people understood the meaning of desire, this objection would not have arisen from them. Desire means that you know the truth, but your desire turns you away from it. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) did not know a ruling in these matters and then turned away from it; rather, he spoke and judged according to what he understood in a matter on which nothing had come down from God. Then the ruling came down from God to amend the ijtihad of His Messenger.

So then: the Messenger of God had no desire to speak according to. In God's amending of His Messenger, and the Messenger's conveying of this amendment to his community, is the greatest evidence of his truthfulness (ﷺ) and his trustworthiness in conveying from his Lord. Otherwise, no one would have known of this amendment had the Messenger of God concealed it out of partisanship for himself or to ward off error from himself.

Among this is His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿O Prophet, why do you prohibit what God has made lawful for you, seeking the approval of your wives..﴾ (66:1), and He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿May God pardon you. Why did you give them permission..﴾ (9:43).

The Messenger of God could have concealed these verses that rebuke him and count as a reproach against him, but he (ﷺ) was a trustworthy man who said what was for him and what was against him. Therefore his Lord says of him: ﴿And if he had attributed to Us some sayings (44) We would have seized him by the right hand (45) Then We would have cut from him the aorta (46)﴾ (69:44-46).

Then He, the Exalted, says: ﴿Rather, We have brought them their reminder, but they, from their reminder, are turning away (71)﴾ (23:71). The word "bal" (rather) indicates a turning away from the preceding speech and the affirmation of new speech after it. The "reminder" here means: honour, renown, and high standing, as in His saying about the Qur'an: ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for you and your people..﴾ (43:44).

And His saying: ﴿We have certainly revealed to you a Book in which is your reminder. Then will you not reason? (10)﴾ (21:10). It was obligatory upon them to embrace this Qur'an and raise it above their heads, for in it is their glory, honour, and might. The Arabs without the Qur'an have no reputation. They were an unlettered people living on wandering and migration, settling only at water sources and pasturage. They were Bedouins among whom wars, raids, and highway robbery spread; one of them would steal in order to honour his guest with what he had stolen.

This is among the astonishing customs of the Arabs in the pre-Islamic era. They had no method governing their lives. It is remarkable that love of raiding and aggression exists together with chivalry and generosity in one nature. He does whatever occurs to him and whatever comes to his mind; the matter is not governed among them by any law. So a poet said of them: "Do not praise Ibn 'Abbad, though his palm pours rain, until he resembles the rain-cloud in generosity. Those are impulses from his whisperings: he gives and withholds, not out of stinginess nor out of generosity."

Among the most famous poems of Arabic verse on generosity is this poem in which this trait is rooted even among children, and in which a father is about to slaughter his son for a guest, because he did not find anything to slaughter to entertain him.

The poet says in it: "Hungry for three nights, his belly bound, dusty with sand, in a desert where no one had known a trace... A brother whose loneliness had something of intimacy, whose harshness saw in him misery as a blessing. He saw a figure in the midst of darkness and was frightened; then, when he saw a guest, he girded himself and was concerned. He said: 'O my Lord, a guest and no hospitality! By Your right, do not deprive him of meat tonight.' He set apart in a ravine an old woman before him, and three figures, you would think them... barefoot, naked, who had not eaten bread of the ash-baked kind, nor known the taste of wheat since they were created." Then his son, when he saw him perplexed, said: "Father, slaughter me and prepare food for them. Do not excuse yourself with poverty before the one who thinks we have wealth, lest he reproach us." So he rested a little, then hesitated for a while, and if he did not slaughter his youth, he would have been dismayed. While they were thus, a wild ass appeared from afar, arranged behind its leader in a line, thirsty and seeking water, and it slipped toward them though it was thirsty to its own blood. He gave it respite until its thirsty ones had quenched their thirst, and he shot an arrow at it from his quiver. It fell toward a fat she-ass with a foal, filled with flesh and layered with fat. Glad tidings to him when he dragged it toward his people, and glad tidings to them when they saw its wound bleeding. Their father spent the night, from his cheerfulness, a father to his guests, and the mother from her joy a mother."

The trait of generosity has taken deep root in the Arab, even among young children. Though he is poor, he does not like to be known for poverty; he wishes to appear as a wealthy, generous, giving man, even if that contradicts other blameworthy qualities in him.

The point is that they were a people whose traits were contradictory, and they lived in complete unlettered illiteracy, not having cultivated a civilization. This was credited to them after the emergence of Islam and the mission of the Prophet (ﷺ) from among them. How could such people bring these lofty meanings and expressions which govern the whole world? Had they been people of knowledge and civilization, they would have said of them and of Islam: it is a civilizational leap.

Had the Messenger of God (ﷺ) been a reader, they would have said: he read from so-and-so and so-and-so, as the Truth, glory be to Him, related of them: ﴿And We certainly know that they say, "It is only a human who teaches him..﴾ (16:103).

So then: the reminder, honour, glory, and dignity of the Arabs in the Qur'an, yet they did not act even for their own benefit, did not care for this Qur'an, but turned away from it: ﴿but they, from their reminder, are turning away (71)﴾ (23:71), i.e., from the Qur'an. This is evidence that they were heedless, not even knowing their own benefit.

1 - Narrated by Ibn Abi 'Asim in the book "al-Sunnah" (1/12) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr, and Ibn Rajab al-Hanbali cited it in "Jami' al-'Ulum wa al-Hikam" (p. 460) and declared it weak.
2 - al-Watin: a vein in the heart, if it is severed the person dies; it is the main vital artery that feeds the body with pure blood leaving the heart. The meaning: We would have quickly ended him and destroyed him swiftly if he contravened Our command in any way. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/319]
3 - He is Isma'il ibn 'Abbad Abu al-Qasim al-Taliqani, a minister dominated by literature, appointed as vizier by Mu'ayyad al-Dawla and then by his brother Fakhr al-Dawla, and called "al-Sahib" for his companionship with Mu'ayyad al-Dawla from his youth. Born in Taliqan (of the districts of Qazvin) in 326 AH, to which he is attributed, he died in Rayy (Tehran) in 385 AH and was transferred to Isfahan and buried there. [al-A'lam by al-Zirikli 1/316]
4 - al-Dima: rain without thunder or lightning, i.e., persistent rain. It is said: the sky persisted (dama tadim): it rained a dima. [Lisan al-'Arab, root: d-y-m]
5 - al-Qara: food for guests.
6 - al-Ta'wi: the hungry one. Murmil: whose food is mixed with sand. al-Rasm: a trace.
7 - Ra'ahu: frightened him and alarmed him.
8 - Khubz mulla: bread placed in hot ash that has been heated so that the bread is buried in it to cook.
9 - 'Anat: appeared. 'Anah: the wild ass among animals, of wild asses. al-Mishal: the leader of the herd.
10 - Nahwas: fat and full. Tabaqat shahman: became filled with fat and flesh.
11 - al-Kalm: the wound. Yadma: bleeds blood. [See Lisan al-'Arab]

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿Or do you ask them for a payment? But the payment of your Lord is better, and He is the best of providers.﴾ (23:72)

(Al-Kharj): that which comes out of you willingly. As for al-Kharaj (tax, levy), it is that which comes out of you against your will. An increase in the form of a word indicates an increase in its meaning, so al-Kharaj is more intensive than al-Kharj. The meaning of His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Or do you ask them for a payment? But the payment of your Lord is better...﴾ [al-Mu'minun]: if you want a payment (kharj), do not take it from their hands; take it from your Lord. What they have is not a kharj but a kharaj. ﴿But the payment of your Lord is better...﴾ [al-Mu'minun].

So take provision only from the hand of goodness and blessing, because the Truth, glorified is He, does not bestow favour upon His creation by providing for them. Rather, He, glorified is He, has summoned them to life, and therefore He has undertaken their provision, just as if you invited a friend to a meal and prepared enough for ten people. So what of when your Lord, Mighty and Majestic, prepares for you?

Then the Truth, glorified is He, concludes the verse with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and He is the best of providers﴾ [al-Mu'minun]. This has raised a difficulty for some, because the Truth, glorified is He, has given His creatures a share in the attribute of provision, since others also provide. But He is the best of providers, because He provides creatures with the origins of the things from which they provide others. If you provide someone else with food, for example, He, glorified is He, is the origin and source of that food.

He, glorified is He, is the Creator of the soil, the Creator of the water, the Creator of the air, and the Creator of the seed. All that is required of you is that you use your mind and the energies that God has granted you, and so you bring forth this food. If you were to bring your household the kitchen supplies and necessities for the whole month, such as flour, ghee, rice, sugar, and so on, and your wife then prepared the food, would you say that the wife is the one who brought the food?

Therefore the scholars and people of knowledge say: purify your tongues from saying "so-and-so is a provider," and leave that to the saying of God Almighty, because He, glorified is He, is the Creator of provision and the Originator of its sources, and you are merely a conveyor of it to others.

You also notice that He, Exalted is He, attributed the payment to the lordship (rububiyyah), which implies care, attention and nurturing. So since it is the payment of your Lord, O Muhammad, it is a great payment and a gift that never runs out.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 23, verse 73:

﴿And indeed, you are calling them to a straight path.﴾ (23:73)

As-sirat al-mustaqim (the straight path): the moderate way in which there is no crookedness and no amt (unevenness). How, then, do they refuse you and stand in your way while you call them to the straight path? Even if one person benefits from the crooked path, millions will benefit from the straight path.

Among this is what we have previously explained: that you must look at what the legislation (al-tashri') gives you before you look at what it takes from you. The Shari'ah, when it takes from you while you are rich, gives to you while you are poor, and it commands you to care for the orphan so that he may care for your children after you if you leave them while they are young.

So the Shari'ah secures your life and makes you receive the decrees of Allah with contentment, because you are in a faithful society that will not abandon you if you become poor, and will not leave your children if they become orphans. In a faithful society, if the father dies, everyone becomes a father to the orphan. But if the orphan is lost in a society of faith, that opens the door to discontent with the decree of Allah, and tempts those of weak faith to say: "What is the wisdom in His taking their father and leaving them as dependents whom no one looks after?"

1 - Al-amt (unevenness): difference in a place in height and depth. From it is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿You will not see therein any crookedness or unevenness﴾ (20:107), meaning: on the Day of Resurrection you will not see in the earth any twisting or deviation to the right or left, nor will you see in it any difference in height and depth; that is, it will be perfectly level, vertically and horizontally. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/30]..

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 23, verse 74:

﴿And indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter are deviating from the path.﴾ (23:74):

﴿The path...﴾ [al-Mu'minun] (74): It is the straight way that leads to the goal with the least effort and in the shortest time, and brings you to the best goal. The way takes its share of care and attention in proportion to the goal it leads to. So the road from Cairo to Alexandria is not like the road between villages and hamlets.

And the meaning of ﴿deviating﴾ [al-Mu'minun] (74): that is, they veer away from the path, and they have a share of crookedness and lack of uprightness. For this reason, one who wants to speak truthfully says to you (ta'āl dōghri), meaning: come straight, along the straight path that has no crookedness and no evasion.

But what made them swerve from the straight path that organizes the movement of life for them, makes it support one another rather than conflict, and returns the effort of the individual to the others? Why do they deprive themselves of the advantages of this path?

They said: Because they deny the Hereafter. Had they not denied the Hereafter, they would have believed and followed the method of God, because they will return to God in a return that gives the one who does good his reward and gives the one who does evil his recompense. What corrupted these people is that they followed their desires, and thought that this world is the goal and the end of the journey, and they neglected the Hereafter, and that it is the abode of true bliss, which will neither escape you nor you escape it.

As the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, said about it: ﴿And indeed, the Hereafter—that is the [true] life, if they only knew.﴾ (29:64) That is: the true life.

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿And if We had mercy upon them and removed what harm they have, they would persist in their transgression, wandering blindly.﴾ (23:75)

Meaning: if this were to happen, they would return to what they were upon, just as He, glorified is He, said in another place: ﴿And when harm touches man, he calls upon Us, lying on his side or sitting or standing. But when We remove from him his harm, he passes on as if he had never called upon Us to remove a harm that touched him...﴾ (10:12)

Would that he stopped at this limit! Rather, it goes further, as came in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they attribute to Allah equals...﴾ (39:8). He says, as Qarun said: ﴿I was only given it because of knowledge I have...﴾ (28:78). Meaning: this is by my own effort and toil, and I have spoken to so-and-so and done such-and-such.

Therefore it was natural that his Lord would say to him: since you were given it because of knowledge you have, then preserve it with the knowledge you have. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So We caused the earth to swallow him and his home...﴾ (28:81).

Where then is your knowledge now? And what kind of knowledge is this that cannot keep what it has brought? It is well known that deriving a thing is harder than preserving and safeguarding it.

As for the meaning of ﴿persist (lajjū)﴾ (23:75): they persisted (tamadaw). ﴿In their transgression (ṭughyānihim)﴾ (23:75): transgression (al-ṭughyān) is exceeding the limit, because God, exalted is He, has set for everything in existence a fixed limit that it neither falls short of nor exceeds. If you follow this limit which God has drawn for you, you remain upright, and the movement of your life becomes upright without dispute. But if a thing transgresses, it corrupts the movement of life, even water, from which God made every living thing, if it transgresses, drowns and destroys, after having been the secret of life while in balance. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, when the water overflowed, We carried you in the sailing vessel﴾ (69:11).

One who exceeds the limit is called ṭāghiyah, with the feminine ending denoting intensity; if he exceeds even this, we say ṭāghūt.

Then the result of persisting in transgression is ﴿wandering blindly (yaʿmahūn)﴾ (23:75): meaning, they become bewildered and blind to right guidance and correctness, so they cannot distinguish between good and evil.

1 - al-Jāriyah: the ship. Jarat al-safīnah jaryan: the ship sailed. [Lisan al-Arab, root j-r-y].

Then the Truthful, glorified is He, says:

﴿And We had already seized them with punishment, yet they did not humble themselves before their Lord, nor did they supplicate.﴾ (23:76)

Istakana (to be humbled, to submit) is not said except of one who was moving in an evil motion and then calmed down and became still. We say: "So-and-so (inkana) or istakana," and its root is (kawn). The meaning is that he sought a new existence other than the existence he had been in, or a state other than the state he had been in at first. Thus, before he becomes humble and submits, he must have been rebellious against his Lord.

Existence is of two kinds: primary absolute existence, and secondary existence following the primary existence. For example, we say: "Zayd was born," meaning Zayd came into existence in the primary sense. But in what form did he come into existence? Beautiful or ugly? This requires another existence. You say: "Zayd was thus, he did so-and-so," and the doer does not need another report, because it refers to the first existence. But when we say: "Zayd was diligent (mujtahidan)," this is the second existence, which is diligence, and it is an existence resulting from the first existence.

Thus kāna here is the complete kāna (kāna al-tāmmah) found in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if the debtor is in hardship, then [grant him] postponement until [a time of] ease...﴾ (2:280): that is, "there came into existence a debtor in hardship," and in this case it does not need a predicate.

And we say: "So-and-so wished from God that a child would come into existence for him, so Muhammad was" — meaning: came into existence. But the incomplete kāna (kāna al-nāqisah) requires a predicate, because kāna is a verb indicating past time, and a verb must indicate a time and an event; therefore it requires a predicate that gives the event. You say: "Zayd was diligent," so the predicate came to complete the incomplete verb, as if you had said: "Zayd is diligent."

The meaning of ﴿So they did not humble themselves before their Lord﴾ (23:76) is that their humility and submission were not for themselves nor for people; rather, humility before God means receiving His commands with utmost humility and utmost obedience. But they did not do so, neither in a state of mercy and removal of harm, nor in a state of seizure and punishment. It was incumbent upon them to know that God had changed His dealing with them, and the consequence of that was that they should also change their own condition toward God, by humbling themselves before their Lord and submitting to His commands.

﴿Nor did they supplicate﴾ (23:76): ḍarāʿah (supplication) is calling upon, lowliness, and submission to one who holds your hand in something, as in His saying: ﴿So why, when Our might came upon them, did they not supplicate?﴾ (6:43). That is: they sought refuge in God and turned to Him with supplication and appeal for help.

1 – Occasion of revelation of the verse: Ibn ʿAbbās said: It was revealed concerning the story of Thumāmah ibn Uthāl, when a military detachment captured him, and he embraced Islam, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) released him. He prevented Mecca from receiving grain from al-Yamāmah, and said: "By God, not a grain of wheat will come to you from al-Yamāmah until the Messenger of God (ﷺ) permits it." God seized Quraysh with famine and hunger, until they ate carrion, dogs, and al-ʿalhiz. It was said: "What is al-ʿalhiz?" He said: "They would take wool and hair, soak it in blood, then roast it and eat it." Then Abū Sufyān said to him: "I implore you by God and by kinship: do you not claim that God sent you as a mercy to the worlds?" He said: "Yes." He said: "By God, I see you have only killed the fathers by the sword and the sons by hunger." Then the verse was revealed: ﴿And even if We had mercy upon them and removed what harm was upon them, they would persist in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾ (23:75). Reported by al-Qurṭubī in his tafsīr (6/4677) and al-Wāḥidī in Asbāb al-Nuzūl (p. 179).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 23, verse 77:

﴿Until, when We open upon them a gate of severe punishment, behold, they will be in despair therein.﴾ (23:77):

All attempts with them have failed. Mercy did not benefit them, and they persisted in their insolence. Punishment did not avail them either, and they did not humble themselves after Allah had seized them with it. Therefore, no argument remained for them and no hope of salvation, so Allah opened upon them ﴿a gate of severe punishment…﴾ (23:77). That is: a trial befell them, as if they were behind a closed door that suddenly surprised them. ﴿Behold, they will be in despair therein﴾ (23:77): they will be hopeless of deliverance and full of regret over what they have missed.

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, says:

﴿It is He who brought into being for you hearing, sight and hearts; little are you grateful.﴾ (78)

Al-Haqq, glory be to Him and exalted, says: I created My servants from nothing, and I supplied them with the means of sustenance and the necessities of life from nothing. Then I made for them a method (manhaj) that regulates the movement of their lives and preserves their structure, because the maker of a thing knows his making best, knows what sets it right, and knows the purpose for which he created it. Take the refrigerator, for example: did the one who made it first make it and then tell us, "Look into what use this device is to you"? No. Rather, before making it, he defined its task and its purpose. So too is the creation of God, and to God belongs the highest likeness.

He who created and defined the purpose knows the law of maintenance that protects His creation from corruption and makes it perform its task in the most perfect way. If you oppose the law of maintenance which your Lord has laid down for you, your life will be corrupted and you will be disabled from performing the task for which you were created, which is the worship of God alone, without partner: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat]. (56)

Therefore He has commanded you, if you dispute about anything, to refer it back to God and the Messenger, just as a device is referred back to its maker, who knows its nature and the places of fault in it. From this matter we derive: if you see a defect in the universe or corruption in one of its aspects, and if you see some shameful thing has appeared, know that a ruling of God has been suspended.

For example, if you see a poor man hungry and naked, either he is able to work but has sat idle from striving, contrary to the words of God: ﴿So walk in its pathways and eat of His provision, and to Him is the resurrection﴾ [al-Mulk] (15); or: the able and working people have deprived him of his right which God made for him in their wealth, contrary to the words of God: ﴿And in their wealth there is a right for the beggar and the deprived﴾ [al-Dhariyat]. (19)

Therefore, the Truth, glory be to Him, brings upon His servants such decrees as preserve for them the balance of life and meet the needs of the needy. As we see, for example, a wealthy man leaves his country and moves to another country, where he places his money and wealth, and there is no cause for this move except that it is a venture which God has set upon him in order to preserve the distribution of wealth in society. If you were to calculate it, you would find that in this place the zakat yield exceeded the needs of the needy, so he moved to another country where wealth decreased below the needs of the poor and the needy.

After that, your Lord has not left you alone; rather He has presented to you the signs that turn you towards Him and move you to come to know Him. These are either wondrous cosmic signs that point to the power of God, or miracles that establish the truthfulness of the prophets in conveying from God, because God does not address each of His servants individually; rather He sends a messenger to convey to them, then supports him with a miracle that shows the truth of his message.

So when you look at the signs of the universe and infer from them the existence of a powerful Creator, but you do not know who this Creator is, the Messenger comes to tell you: it is God. We have given an example of this, and to God belongs the highest likeness: suppose someone knocked on the door while we were sitting inside. What happens? We all agree that someone is at the door. But who is he? No one knows.

So the agreement here is in reason, that there is a force behind the door knocking, but who is it? And what does he want? To know these matters, there must be a message from this force. Beware of saying by conjecture: "This is so-and-so," and I say, "This is so-and-so." Rather, we must wait for the message from him to know who he is. All you have to say is: "Who is at the door?" and he himself will tell you about himself, about the reason for his coming, and what he wants. Then after that come the verses that carry God's method and tell you that He wants this and that from you.

The point: all these signs need means of perception. They need hearing and sight so we may see and hear them, and then they need reason so we may think upon and contemplate them. Therefore He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿It is He who brought into being for you hearing, sight and hearts...﴾ (78) [al-Mu'minun].

Hearing and sight are among the senses which the scholars called, as a precaution, the five outward senses; that is, there are other senses which they have not discovered, and indeed science later discovered them, such as the muscular sense by which weight is distinguished, and the sense of pressure by which, for example, the thick is distinguished from the thin in cloth. These things you cannot recognize by the five known senses.

The chief of the senses is hearing and sight, because when a messenger comes to me conveying from God, I must hear from him. If I am a believer in a god, I have been sufficed by the sense of hearing; and if I am an unbeliever, I need sight to see His signs which indicate His existence and power, and to infer the made from the maker and the creation from the Creator, and to stand upon what is in God's universe of precision, firmness, engineering and innovation.

This is the task of reason, after the heard and seen things have turned into rational propositions and principles that govern your life. For example, if you saw fire with your eye, then touched it with your hand and it burned you, there forms in you a rational proposition whose content is that fire has the property of burning, so you do not touch it afterwards. This you see even in a small child, when he is pleased by a chili pepper, for example, bites it, and feels its heat and pain.

Then when he sees it afterwards he says "ouf." For the child, this word is a rational proposition formed as a result of an experience that settled in his heart, and he took it as a principle to follow throughout his life. Likewise, from the sensible things and the experiences of life, rational propositions form in you which you benefit from afterwards.

Thus: from the means of perception arise principles and propositions which reason takes up and weighs among, until it ends at a proposition and principle that settles in the heart, which we call 'aqidah, meaning: something tied firmly that does not come undone.

When you reflect on the Qur'an's discourse about the senses, you find that it always arranges them in this order: hearing, sight, and the heart, because they are the chief of the senses. Smell, taste and touch, for example, we need only a little; but hearing and sight are the basis of the matter of the call: hearing to hear the message, and sight to see God's signs which indicate His power, exalted is He.

Modern science has confirmed this order of hearing, sight and heart, which indicates that it is an order from a Creator of wisdom, knowledge and power, such that none of them comes before the other. Physiologists have likewise confirmed the truth of this order: the first organ to perform its task in man is the ear, then the eye, and they function from three to ten days after birth; then from hearing and sight arise the propositions in which reason works.

Therefore, this order is innate and constitutional. Hearing, which is the first sense to perform its task in man, is also the only perception that accompanies man through all his stages: the ear hears even in sleep, unlike the eye, because through hearing the summoning takes place, so it continues to perform its task even in sleep.

Also, the eye does not see in darkness, and it has a natural covering and closures that block vision; the ear is not like that. When a sound goes out, all ears hear it, whereas the visible may be present with you in the same place and you do not see it while another sees it. Therefore the heard is one, while the seen is many. For this reason He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿the hearing and the sights...﴾ (78) [al-Mu'minun].

You have no choice in hearing, but you have a choice in seeing: visible things multiply with the multiplicity of eyes, but hearing does not multiply with the multiplicity of ears.

For this reason, among the miraculous features of Qur'anic expression in the story of the People of the Cave, God, exalted is He, struck upon their ears in the cave so that they might sleep and the sounds of this wide desert would not disturb them. Had hearing remained for them as it is for all creation, rest would not have settled for them throughout this long period, and sounds would have terrified them.

The Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, says: ﴿So We struck upon their ears in the cave for a number of years﴾ [al-Kahf]. (11)

Also among the signs of inimitability in the Noble Qur'an: all the verses that mention hearing and sight mention them in this order, hearing then sight, except in one verse, in the situation of the Resurrection, where they say: ﴿Our Lord, we have seen and we have heard...﴾ (12) [al-Sajdah]: here sight is placed before hearing, because in the Resurrection the visible surprises them first before the sounds surprise them. This is one of the manifestations of precision in the inimitable Qur'anic expression.

It is as if the Truth, glory be to Him, is saying: You have no excuse with Me. I gave you hearing to hear the message from Me through the Messenger, I gave you an eye to turn to the signs of the universe, and I gave you a heart with which to reflect, and to arrive at a faith-yielding result that guides you to the existence of the Creator, mighty and majestic.

Therefore: I did not seize you unawares, nor did I deceive you in anything. Rather, I created you from nothing, supplied you from nothing, and arranged for you the channels of perception in a logical, constitutional order. So what excuse will you have after that? Beware, after all this, that desires should not occupy you and divert you from the message that came to you by the tongue of Our Messenger.

Whoever reflects on the construction of both the ear and the eye finds in them signs and miracles of the Creator, mighty and majestic, whose secrets and essence scientists have still not reached despite the advance of knowledge.

Then He, glory be to Him, says at the end of the verse: ﴿little are you grateful﴾ (78) [al-Mu'minun]: because these are blessings, bounties and signs from God, you ought to be grateful with the true gratitude.

Some say concerning the meaning of ﴿little are you grateful﴾ (78): that He expressed the absence of gratitude by the word "little." This understanding does not hold here, because God has affirmed for His servants some gratitude, but it is little; and your Lord, mighty and majestic, desires constant gratitude accompanying every blessing He bestows upon you. When you see the blind man who has been deprived of the blessing of sight stumbling along the road, you say "Praise be to God," saying it naturally, because you live and move within God's blessings, but you do not remember them except when you see those who have been deprived of them.

Therefore, if you wish the blessing to endure, then bind it by remembering God the Bestower. Say at the blessing, or when you see something that pleases you in family or wealth: "What God wills; there is no power except through God." Do you not see that God made envy so as to alert us? If you want to preserve the blessing, do not forget the Bestower, for He alone is able to keep and preserve it, just as we now buy a machine and agree with its maker on periodic maintenance for a specific fee.

Likewise, if you say at the blessing: "What God wills; there is no power except through God," you will never see any harm in it, because by "What God wills; there is no power except through God" you have awakened the law of its maintenance, and you have entrusted its preservation to the One who made it. A person is only afflicted in a blessing when he is heedless of the Bestower and neglects to thank Him for it.

I recall that in our village there was a man of understanding regarding God, who owned a third of a feddan which he planted with traditional crops. In one year he planted it with cotton, and the worm came upon it and nearly destroyed it. My father spoke to him about this worm matter, and he said: "O uncle Mutawalli, do not worry, for I am performing its maintenance," meaning: I take zakat out of it.

Then the Truthful, Glorified One says:

﴿And it is He who created you (dispersed you) upon the earth, and to Him you will be gathered.﴾ (79)

{ {dhara'akum...} (79) [al-Mu'minun]: We scattered you and spread you throughout the regions of the earth, so that it would all be inhabited. And you marvel when you see people clinging to the mountains and the barren, parched deserts, who do not accept any substitute for them, and who bear hardship and difficulty in the pursuit of remaining there, to the point that you say: "Why do they not leave this place for a fertile one?"

We have seen such people who were patient with the decrees of God in their lands. We saw them in Yemen after the flood of al-Arim had drowned it, and it was called "Happy Yemen." We saw them in Saudi Arabia and in Kuwait, and the people of these lands related to us the constriction and harshness of life they had endured. Then the outcome of their patience came to them, and God, glorified and exalted be He, made these mountains and these deserts the richest lands of the world, because they were content in the former with God's decree. So He exchanged for their patience over the hardships of the desert a bounty which, if the affluent of the world were deprived of it, they would die of cold.

That is because the Creator, mighty and majestic, scattered His bounties across all regions of the earth equally, so that every longitudinal stretch of earth contains bounties like those in another stretch. At one time, the people of cultivation were the people of wealth and lordship, then this situation changed with the emergence of other bounties besides agriculture. Thus, bounties are buried throughout the regions of the earth, but each has a time in which it appears.

Therefore, the dispersal and spreading of creation throughout the regions of the earth has a wisdom which the Creator, mighty and majestic, intended.

Then He, glorified be He, says: ﴿And to Him you will be gathered.﴾ (79) [al-Mu'minun]: That is: do not think that by your being spread across the earth and separated within it, you will escape from Us, or that We are unable to gather you again. Just as We spread you for a wisdom, We will gather you for a wisdom, and no one escapes from Our hands.

Then the Almighty says:

﴿It is He who gives life and causes death, and His is the alternation of the night and the day. Will you not then use your reason?﴾ (80)

﴿He gives life and causes death..﴾ (80) [al-Mu'minun]: These are two verbs that must come into being after the existence of life and the existence of death. So the Creator, Exalted is He, brings life into existence first, brings death into existence, and then sets an event from both of them in motion as He wills.

Life precedes death in every verse, except for one verse in Surah Tabarak: ﴿He who created death and life..﴾ (2) [al-Mulk]. The reason for this is that Allah, Exalted is He, gives the human being, through life, a will that initiates movement in all his organs. Consider: what do you do if you want to stand up from your place? What do you do if you want to move your hand or your foot? It is merely a will, and your limbs move without your knowing, or exerting yourself to perform these movements, and without your handling anything at all.

So: by the mere exercise of your will, your limbs respond to you, while you are a creature of your Lord. If the creature does what it wills without effort, how then do we find this improbable in regard to Him, glory be to Him and exalted, and deny that He says to a thing: "Be," and it is? Yet we do what we will with our limbs by the mere act of willing, without commanding them with anything or saying anything, whereas Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, says to a thing: "Be," and it is. You act without speaking.

The Almighty placed death first in this verse: ﴿He who created death and life..﴾ (2) [al-Mulk], because life would bring a person the delusion that his will controls his limbs, so he would become arrogant. So his Lord, Exalted is He, wanted to alert him: remember that I cause death, so that he would receive life together with its opposite, and so remain upright in the movement of life.

The attributes of creating and causing death are attributes of Allah that are eternal, before He created anything or caused anything to die, because they are established attributes of Allah before He actually exercises what these attributes relate to, as we have said. And to Allah belongs the highest likeness: the poet, when he says a poem, says it because he is a poet, and we do not say that he is a poet because he said this poem; for were it not for the attribute of poetry in him, he would not have said it.

Just as life is created, death is likewise created. Someone may say: if I fire a bullet at a person and make him a corpse, then I have created death. We say: praise be to Allah that you did not claim to give life and were content with causing death. But there is a difference between death and killing. Killing is the breaking down of the structure, followed by the taking away of the soul; whereas in death, the soul departs first without the structure being broken down.

Therefore the Almighty says: ﴿Muhammad is but a messenger; messengers have passed away before him. So if he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?..﴾ (144) [Al 'Imran].

Nimrod, who argued with Ibrahim (peace be upon him) about his Lord, ordered one man to be killed and spared another, and claimed that he had given life to this one and caused that one to die. These acts of his were sophistry without any meaning. Had he been upon the truth, he would have ordered the one he had killed to be brought back to life. Therefore Ibrahim (peace be upon him) cut off this path for him and moved him to another field in which he could not evade.

So: the destruction of the structure is followed by the departure of the soul, because the soul has special specifications, such that it does not dwell except in a sound structure. We have clarified this matter, and to Allah belongs the highest likeness, by the example of an electric bulb: the power of electricity lies dormant in the wires, and we do not see its light until we place the bulb in its place; and it has specifications such that it does not shine except when these specifications are available to it. If it is broken, its light goes out.

Then He, exalted, says: ﴿and His is the alternation of the night and the day..﴾ (80) [al-Mu'minun]. The night arrives with the sun's setting and the coming of darkness which prevents the seeing of things. In olden times they thought that sight occurs when a ray issues from the eye and falls upon the object seen. Then the Muslim scholar al-Hasan ibn al-Haytham came and proved the error of this theory, and established that sight occurs when a ray from the object falls upon the eye so that you see it, as proof that you do not see a thing if it is in darkness.

The darkness of night alerts us to the importance of the light which is indispensable for us to be guided in the movement of life. A person faces danger if he walks in the dark, for he may either collide with someone weaker than himself and crush him, or with someone stronger who will hurt and harm him.
