You may have no friends, no companions, and no colleagues at work, but you must have lineage, kinship, and family.

When the Truth, glory be to Him, negates lineage, He says: ﴿there will be no kinship among them..﴾ [al-Mu'minun]. The negation is not of the existence of lineage. When the Trumpet is blown, the connection of sonship to fatherhood, or of fatherhood to sonship, is cut off. Lineage truly exists, but because the known benefit of lineage is mutual help toward good and mutual support in repelling evil, the negation here refers to this benefit on this very day, when no one benefits anyone else. So lineage exists, but without benefit. In worldly affairs, benefit arises because there is a strong person and a weak person, and the strong helps and bestows upon the weak. But in this situation, everyone is weak.

As He, the Exalted, said: ﴿On the Day when a man will flee from his brother, and from his mother and his father, and from his spouse and his children, each one of them that Day will have a matter that occupies him.﴾ [Abasa 34-37].

And He says: ﴿Every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned.﴾ [al-Muddaththir 38].

Therefore, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) related to us that we will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection barefoot, naked and uncircumcised, Aisha was astonished and felt shy at this situation. The Messenger of Allah informed her that the matter was not so, for this is a situation in which each person is preoccupied with himself, and the state is too severe for anyone to look at anyone else.(1)

So the negation is of the benefit of lineages, not of lineages themselves.

If the benefit of lineage is ruled out by the terror of the Hereafter, a person may still rise above and withhold his benefit even in this world from his close relatives if they are not believers. Allah has set this as an example in the story of Noah, peace be upon him, and his son, when his Lord addressed him: ﴿He is not of your family; indeed, his deed is unrighteous..﴾ [Hud 46]. Thus lineage was negated even in this world. Sonship is not sonship of blood and flesh; sonship, especially among the prophets, is sonship of deed and following.

If you reflect on the history of the early Muslims, you will find that they took pride in Islam, not in lineages. Religion and creed are the bond, and they are the strong tie that connects a person to others, even if that person is lower than him by the measures of worldly life.

We read in the story of Badr that Mus'ab ibn Umayr(2), may Allah be pleased with him, was the pampered youth of Quraysh and the wealthiest of its wealthy. He wore the finest garments and lived the softest life. When faith permeated his heart, he renounced all this luxury and was deprived of the best of his family. Then he emigrated to Madinah, and there the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw him wearing a sheepskin, and said: "Look what faith has done to your brother."(3)

In the battle, Mus'ab saw his brother Abu Aziz(4) taken captive in the hand of one of the Ansar, the Companion Abu al-Yusr(5). Mus'ab said to him: "Bind your captive firmly, meaning: beware lest he escape from you, for his mother is wealthy and will ransom him with much wealth." Abu Aziz looked at Mus'ab and said: "Is this your charge concerning your brother?" He replied: "This one is my brother rather than you."

So there is no kinship among them, even in this world before the Hereafter.

In the Battle of Uhud, Mus'ab ibn Umayr was martyred, and they found nothing to shroud him in except a short garment: if it covered his head, his feet were exposed, and if it covered his feet, his head was exposed. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Cover his head, and place idhkhir (a fragrant grass) over his feet."(6)

When Umm Habiba bint Abi Sufyan embraced Islam and emigrated with her husband to Abyssinia, some accused her of having emigrated not for the sake of her religion but for the sake of her husband. Allah willed to demonstrate her innocence: her husband, Ubayd Allah ibn Jahsh, became a Christian there, while she remained upon faith. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) learned of her situation, he wished to compensate her, so he proposed to her on his own behalf, without waiting for her to come to him to conclude the contract. He appointed al-Najashi, the king of Abyssinia, as his agent to conclude the marriage for him.(7)

After her marriage to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), her father Abu Sufyan wished to visit her, and she was spreading out the bedding of the Messenger of Allah. When Abu Sufyan wanted to sit on it, she pulled it away from him and prevented him from sitting, being a disbeliever, on the bedding of the Messenger of Allah. He said: "Do you begrudge the bedding to me?" She said: "Yes."(8)

So the benefit of lineage is ruled out in this world before it is ruled out in the Hereafter. But the Truth, glory be to Him, graciously kept the requirements of lineage in this world and urged us to preserve them even with disbelievers, because He, glory be to Him, encompasses the disbeliever. So the believer ought to encompass him all the more. If you see a disbeliever in distress and you are able to help him, then help him.

Consider in this regard His saying: ﴿And if they strive with you to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them, but accompany them in this world with kindness..﴾ [Luqman 15].

They are both disbelievers, and indeed they want you to be a disbeliever, yet preserve for them their right of kinship and do not sever your ties with them.

It is related that Ibrahim, peace be upon him, whom Allah had granted the station of close friendship (khullah), and of whom He said: ﴿And Ibrahim, who fulfilled (his covenant)﴾ [al-Najm 37], and whom He tested with words and he fulfilled them, had a passing traveller come to him at night. Before letting him in and hosting him, he asked him about his religion, and the man told him that he was not a believer. Ibrahim, peace be upon him, turned away from him and let him leave. Then Allah revealed to him: "O Ibrahim, you have shown kindness to My servant while he disbelieves in Me, and you want him to change his religion for the sake of one night's hospitality?" Ibrahim hurried after the man until he caught up with him and told him of the rebuke his Lord had addressed to him concerning him. The man said: "What a Lord who rebukes His beloved over the matter of His enemies!" and he testified that there is no god but Allah and that Ibrahim is the Messenger of Allah.

People of knowledge who rise to the understanding of lineage see that it extends beyond the connection caused by your existence, which is father or mother. Lineage, though it is the emergence of one thing from another or the branching of one thing from another, there is a higher lineage: not to the one who brought you into existence through a cause, but to the one who brought you into existence without any cause, the first existence. So it was incumbent upon you to observe this lineage first, the one that brought you from non-existence, even though parents have a rightful claim because they are the cause of your existence. How then with the Supreme Originator?

As for His saying: ﴿and they will not ask one another.﴾ [al-Mu'minun 101]: "Sa'ala" (to ask) requires a questioner and one questioned. The verb "tasa'ala" (to ask one another) indicates reciprocity, meaning each of them asks at one time and is asked at another, as you say: "Muhammad shared with Amr" and "fought" etc.

Some orientalists, who love to find fault with the Book of Allah, have objected to this verse, saying: "Muslims regard the Book of Allah with such reverence and sanctity that it prevents them and blinds their minds from rationally understanding what is in it. Why, when Allah said of the Qur'an: ﴿Had it been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much contradiction﴾ [al-Nisa' 82]?"

These people say: the Qur'an negates questioning in this verse, and affirms it in His saying: ﴿And they will turn to one another, questioning﴾ [al-Tur 25], in the dialogue among the disbelievers.

There is also questioning between the believers and the disbelievers: ﴿Every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned, except the companions of the right, who will be in gardens, asking one another about the guilty, "What led you into Saqar?" They will say: "We were not of those who prayed, nor did we feed the needy, and we used to engage in vain talk with those who engaged in it, and we used to deny the Day of Judgment."﴾ [al-Muddaththir 38-46].

And sometimes the questioning is among the believers themselves: ﴿And they will turn to one another, questioning. They will say: "Indeed, we were before this among our people, fearful. So Allah conferred favor upon us and protected us from the punishment of the scorching wind. Indeed, we used to call upon Him before; indeed, He is the Kind, the Merciful."﴾ [al-Tur 25-28].

So how, after this, does He negate questioning, saying: ﴿and they will not ask one another﴾ [al-Mu'minun 101]?

This apparent contradiction is not real, because there is a difference between hearing about a thing and being confronted with it while you are a disbeliever. They said: ﴿There is nothing but our worldly life; we die and we live, and we will not be resurrected﴾ [al-Mu'minun 37].

So when they are confronted with the blast of the Trumpet, and the Resurrection they used to deny overtakes them, they are struck dumb and astonished, and their tongues are silenced from speech by the severity of their astonishment, for how could they not be, when what they used to deny stands before them suddenly? Then they gradually move from this state until they take it as an accomplished fact from which there is no escape, and then they begin to speak, and some ask others about what they are in and what has befallen them.

So questioning has a time, and negation of questioning has a time. Therefore, regarding such matters, they say that the aspect is separate. If you see one thing affirmed once and negated another time by one speaker, who is attributed to wisdom and freedom from contradiction, know that the aspect is distinct.

Orientalists have raised the same objection concerning the questioning of the people of sin, where He says, affirming their questioning: ﴿Stop them, for they are to be questioned﴾ [al-Saffat 24], and says, negating their questioning: ﴿So on that Day no one will be asked about his sin, neither man nor jinn﴾ [al-Rahman 39]. How can the act be affirmed and negated when the agent is one?

This objection of theirs arises from a lack of understanding of the language of the Qur'an and the Arabic linguistic faculty, or because they merely want to find fault with the Book of Allah and stir up doubts about it. But harm may be beneficial: their doubts and objections have stirred the scholars of the Muslims to confront them, to refute their falsehoods, and to expose their intentions. Our case is like that of one who prepares to meet a disease with a suitable vaccine that gives the body immunity against it.

Our master Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, to whom the Qur'an spoke in agreement with what he wished, saw people kissing the Black Stone, and anticipated that people would speak on this matter, and how religion forbids them from worshipping idols, which are stones, while commanding them to kiss a stone. He, may Allah be pleased with him, would kiss it and say: "By Allah, I know that you are a stone that neither harms nor benefits. Had I not seen the Messenger of Allah kiss you, I would not have kissed you."(9)

He thus drew people's attention to the origin of the legislation: that stoneness has no worship in our religion, but for us there is the Prophet (ﷺ), who legislates for us and whose following is obligatory upon us. This was Umar's response to those who stirred up this trial.

When Umar spoke about the high cost of dowries, and he was inspired, his speech agreeing with the words of the Noble Qur'an, a woman stood before him and debated with him, saying: "You are wrong, O Umar. How can you forbid high dowries when Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And if you have given one of them a great amount, do not take from it anything﴾ [al-Nisa' 20]?"

He acknowledged that a dowry may be a qintar of gold, whereupon Umar, with his lofty stature, said: "A woman was right and Umar was wrong,"(10) to show that no one is great before the law of Allah.

So these are established matters with a foundation, which you must know so that we may respond with them when we are asked about the affairs of our religion.

Returning to the question of the questioning of the people of sin, where the Qur'an negated it once and affirmed it another time: we say that the Qur'an came in the style and manner of the Arabs. In Arabic usage, questioning is either a question from one who is ignorant and wants to know, as a student asks his teacher, or it is a question from one who knows, not to learn from him, but to make him confess to what the questioner wants.

So when Allah negates questioning, do not think that He asks you in order to learn from you; He asks you so that you will confess. Therefore He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿Sufficient is your soul against you this Day as a reckoner﴾ [al-Isra' 14].

So affirming questioning has a meaning, and negating it has a meaning: if it is negated, then the questioning for knowledge from their side is negated; and if it is affirmed, then the questioning for confession from their side is affirmed, so that the proof may be more binding, for confession is the master of proofs.

We have clarified this matter with an example: a negligent student who pretends before his father to be studying, opens his book and nods his head as if reading. When his father asks him, he finds that he has accomplished nothing, and so he says to him: "I studied and I did not study."

Similarly, the Exalted's saying addressed to His Messenger (ﷺ): ﴿And you did not throw when you threw, but Allah threw﴾ [al-Anfal 17]. Thus negation and affirmation occur in a single verse for a single agent, because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took a handful of pebbles and threw them toward the enemies(11), yet could he have reached the eyes of all the enemies with that handful? The act of throwing belongs to the Messenger, and the result and the goal belong to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

1 - On the authority of Aisha, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: Allah will resurrect people on the Day of Resurrection barefoot, naked and uncircumcised. Aisha said: O Messenger of Allah, what about the private parts? He said: "For each one of them, on that Day, there is a matter that occupies him." Narrated by Ahmad in his Musnad (6/90), al-Nasa'i in his Sunan (4/114), and al-Hakim in his Mustadrak (4/564), who said: "Sahih according to the condition of Muslim, though they did not record it."

2 - He is Mus'ab ibn Umayr ibn Hashim ibn Abd Manaf, Abu Muhammad. He emigrated to Abyssinia in both the first and second migrations. The Prophet (ﷺ) sent him to Madinah to teach its Muslims jurisprudence and recite the Qur'an to them. Then he came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with the seventy who met him at the second Pledge of al-Aqabah. Mus'ab had fair skin, was neither tall nor short, and was martyred at the Battle of Uhud. [Safwat al-Safwa 1/205, 206].

3 - On the authority of Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) looked at Mus'ab ibn Umayr approaching, wearing a sheepskin (hide) in which he was dressed. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Look at this man whose heart Allah has illuminated. I saw him between two parents who nourished him with the finest food and drink, but his love for Allah and His Messenger drove him to what you see." Cited by Ibn al-Jawzi in Safwat al-Safwa (1/206). Abu Nu'aym recorded it in al-Hilya (1/108). Al-Iraqi said in his takhrij of the hadiths of the Ihya' (4/295): its chain is good (hasan).

4 - He is Zurara ibn Umayr, brother of Mus'ab ibn Umayr. He had companionship and heard from the Prophet (ﷺ), and the historians of the campaigns agreed that he was captured on the day of Badr. See al-Isaba of Ibn Hajar (biography 753, under kunyas).

5 - His name is Ka'b ibn Amr al-Ansari. He witnessed al-Aqabah and Badr, and has many reports concerning them. He is the one who captured al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib. He was short and had a large belly, and died in Madinah in the year 55 AH. [al-Isaba, biography 1243]. Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar vocalized his kunya (Abu al-Yusr), saying (5/307): "with a fatha on the ya' with two dots and the unmarked letter." He said (7/218): "with two fathas."

6 - Agreed upon. Recorded by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (1276) and Muslim in his Sahih (940), from the hadith of Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, may Allah be pleased with him.

7 - Ibn al-Jawzi said in Safwat al-Safwa (2/31): "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent Amr ibn Umayya al-Damri to al-Najashi, king of Abyssinia, to propose to her on his behalf. He married her to him, and al-Najashi gave her dowry on his behalf, four hundred dinars, and sent it to Sharahbil ibn Hasana. It was said: he appointed Khalid ibn Sa'id ibn al-As as his agent, and he married her, and that was in the seventh year of the Hijra."

8 - Cited by Ibn al-Jawzi in Safwat al-Safwa (2/33): "Abu Sufyan said to his daughter Umm Habiba, after she had folded up the bedding of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): 'O daughter, are you averse to this bedding on my account, or to me on account of it?' She said: 'Rather, it is the bedding of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and you are an unclean polytheist man.' He said: 'O daughter, evil has befallen you after me.'" It is well known that Abu Sufyan later embraced Islam at the conquest of Makkah.

9 - Recorded by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (1597) and Muslim in his Sahih (1270), from the hadith of Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him. Al-Tabari said: "Umar only said that because people had recently left the worship of idols, and Umar feared that the ignorant would think that touching the Black Stone is a form of venerating certain stones, as the Arabs used to do in the Jahiliyya. So Umar wanted to teach people that touching it is following the action of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), not because the stone benefits or harms by its own nature, as the Jahiliyya believed about the idols." Cited by Ibn Hajar in al-Fath (3/463).

10 - Cited by Ibn Kathir in his Tafsir (1/467) with the wording "a woman was right and a man was wrong," narrated by al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar. Ibn Kathir said: it contains an interruption (inqita'). He also cited it in a similar form and attributed it to Abu Ya'la. Ibn Kathir said: its chain is good and strong.

11 - From ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah, from Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) raised his hands on the day of Badr and said: 'O Lord, if this band perishes, You will not be worshipped on earth ever again.' Jibrīl said to him: 'Take a handful of dust and throw it into their faces.' So he took a handful of dust and threw it into their faces, and there was not one of the polytheists except that dust from that handful reached his eyes, his nostrils and his mouth, and they turned their backs in flight." Narrated by Abū Nuʿaym (p. 404) and al-Bayhaqī (3/79), both in *Dalāʾil al-Nubuwwah*, and mentioned by Ibn Kathīr in his *Tafsīr* (2/294)..

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 23, verse 102:

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿Then as for those whose scales are heavy, they are the successful. (102) And as for those whose scales are light, they are the ones who have lost their souls, abiding in Hell forever. (103)﴾

Heavy (thaqulat) and light (khaffat) here refer to good deeds: that is, his good deeds were many or they were few. It is possible to say: "his scales became heavy with evil deeds," meaning his good deeds were many, but the Qur'an speaks in terms of the principal matter being good deeds.

The balance (mizan) rests on two pans: in one is the thing weighed (al-mawzun), and in the other is that by which it is weighed (al-mawzun bihi). Weighing has three rational forms: the thing weighed is light, or the thing by which it is weighed is light, or the two are equal. The verse mentions two states: "his scales are light" and "his scales are heavy," as in the words of the Exalted:

﴿As for him whose scales are heavy (6), he will be in a pleasing life (7). But as for him whose scales are light (8), his mother will be the Abyss (9). And what will make you know what it is? (10) A Fire, intensely hot. (11)﴾ [al-Qari'ah]

As for the state of equality, a symbolic allusion to it has come in surah al-A'raf:

﴿And upon the heights are men who recognize each by his mark. They call out to the companions of Paradise, "Peace be upon you," not having entered it, though they hope. (46) And when their sight is turned toward the companions of the Fire, they say, "Our Lord, do not place us with the wrongdoing people." (47)﴾ [al-A'raf]

Whoever's good deeds prevail goes to Paradise, and whoever's evil deeds prevail goes to the Fire, and the people of al-A'raf remain between Paradise and the Fire, because the two pans of their balance are equal: so he is neither of the people of Paradise nor of the people of the Fire. They are on al-A'raf, which is the barrier between Paradise and the Fire, looking at these and at those.

Then the Exalted says concerning them: ﴿They have not entered it, though they hope﴾ [al-A'raf], because God's mercy precedes His wrath, and His pardon precedes His punishment.

The meaning of "heavy" and "light" scales indicates that deeds become, as it were, possessed of density and substance that gives weight; or that God creates for each deed a mass, so that one good deed is weighed as such-and-such. The purpose of the balance is the precision of distinction and reckoning.

We notice in the verse ﴿Then as for those whose scales are heavy... (102)﴾ [al-Mu'minun] that the word is in the plural, "scales" (mawazin), and not "scale" (mizan). Why? They said: because it is possible that each category of deed has its own particular scale: for prayer there is a scale, for wealth a scale, for pilgrimage a scale... and so on, and then all these scales are combined for him.

As for His saying ﴿And as for those whose scales are light, they are the ones who have lost their souls... (103)﴾ [al-Mu'minun]: it is because they took the small, immediate thing and forfeited for themselves the great, deferred thing; they hastened toward a transient enjoyment and abandoned a lasting enjoyment, because the lifespan of this world is limited, time in it is uncertain, and good in it is according to the capacities of its people.

As for the Hereafter, its time is certain, its term is extended and everlasting, and good in it is according to the capacities of the Bountiful, Mighty and Majestic. So if you compare this with that, the extent of what they lost will become clear to you. Therefore the outcome is that they are ﴿abiding in Hell forever (103)﴾ [al-Mu'minun].

Then the Truth, glorified is He, gives us a picture that makes the punishment in Hell appear hideous and depicts its terrors, and this is mercy toward us, so that we may be restrained in time and strive diligently to save ourselves from this destiny and recoil from this dreadful end. Just as the Law (al-shar') states at the outset: "We shall cut off the hand of the thief," it does not want to cut off people's hands; rather, it wants to deter them and warn them of this consequence.

Among that is His saying, concerning the matter of retaliation (qisas): ﴿And for you in retaliation is life, O people of understanding... (179)﴾ [al-Baqarah]:

Retaliation has been much attacked by enemies of Islam, who say: "It is enough that one person from society was killed; why should we kill the other?" The Qur'an did not institute retaliation in order to kill two people; rather, it instituted it to prevent killing, and to preserve both the killer and the killed alive. When the killer knows that he will be killed in retaliation, he refrains and is restrained. If he refrains from killing, then we have given life to both the killer and the killed. They have expressed this meaning by saying: "Retaliation is the most effective deterrent to killing" (al-qatl anfa li-l-qatl).

This is a repeated passage, because it is shared with verse 102: Then the Truthful, glorified is He, says:

﴿Then as for him whose scales are heavy, they are the successful. And as for him whose scales are light, they are the ones who have lost their souls, abiding in Hell.﴾

"Heavy" and "light" here refer to good deeds: either his good deeds were many, or they were few. It could also be said that his scales were heavy with evil deeds, meaning that his good deeds were many, but the Qur'an speaks in terms of the principle that good deeds are the foundation of the matter.

The balance rests on two pans: in one is the thing being weighed, and in the other is the weight used to measure it. There are three rational possibilities for weighing: the thing weighed is light, the measure is light, or the two are equal. The verse mentions two states: "his scales were light" and "his scales were heavy," as in the words of God, exalted is He:

﴿As for him whose scales are heavy, he will be in a pleasing life. And as for him whose scales are light, his refuge will be the Abyss. And what will make you know what it is? A blazing Fire.﴾ [al-Qari'ah]

As for the state of equality, a symbolic indication of it has come in Surat al-A'raf:

﴿And on the heights are men who recognize each by his mark, and they call out to the companions of the Garden, "Peace be upon you." They have not entered it, but they hope. And when their sight is turned toward the companions of the Fire, they say, "Our Lord, do not place us with the wrongdoing people."﴾ [al-A'raf]

Whoever's good deeds prevail goes to Paradise, and whoever's evil deeds prevail goes to the Fire. The people of al-A'raf remain between Paradise and the Fire, because the two pans of the balance are equal for them. So they are neither from the people of Paradise nor from the people of the Fire. They are upon al-A'raf, which is the barrier between Paradise and the Fire, looking at these and at those.

Then God, exalted is He, says concerning them: ﴿They have not entered it, but they hope﴾ [al-A'raf], because the mercy of God has preceded His wrath, and His pardon has preceded His punishment.

The meaning of "his scales were heavy" and "his scales were light" indicates that deeds acquire density and substance that give them weight, or that God creates in every deed a mass, so that a good deed is measured by its own amount. The meaning of the balance is the precision of distinction and reckoning.

We note in the verse ﴿Then as for him whose scales are heavy… (102)﴾ [al-Mu'minun] that the word is in the plural, "scales," and not "scale." Why? They said: because each category of deed may have its own particular scale. So there is a scale for prayer, a scale for wealth, a scale for pilgrimage, and so on, and then all these scales are combined for him.

As for His words: ﴿And as for him whose scales are light, they are the ones who have lost their souls… (103)﴾ [al-Mu'minun], it is because they took the little that is immediate and forfeited for themselves the much that is deferred. They hastened toward a perishing enjoyment and abandoned a lasting one, because the lifespan of this world is limited, time in it is uncertain, and good in it is according to the capacities of its people.

As for the Hereafter, its time is certain, its term is extended and everlasting, and good in it is according to the capacity of the Bestower, mighty and majestic is He. So if you compare this with that, the extent of what they lost will become clear to you. Therefore the outcome is that they are ﴿abiding in Hell (103)﴾ [al-Mu'minun].

Then the Truthful, glorified is He, gives us a picture that makes the recompense in Hell appear hideous and depicts its terrors. This is out of mercy toward us, so that we may be restrained in time, strive earnestly to save ourselves from this destiny, and recoil from this dreadful end. Just as the Law itself states at the outset: "We will cut off the hand of the thief." He does not want to cut off people's hands, but rather to deter them and warn them of this consequence.

Among this is His words, exalted is He, regarding the matter of retaliation (qisas, the law of equal retribution for homicide):

﴿And for you in retribution is life, O people of understanding… (179)﴾ [al-Baqarah]

Retribution has been fiercely attacked by many enemies of Islam, who say: "It is enough that one person was killed from the society; why should we kill the other?" But the Qur'an did not establish retribution in order to kill two people. Rather, it established it to prevent killing, and to preserve both the killer and the one killed alive. When the killer knows that he will be killed in retribution, he refrains and is restrained. If he refrains from killing, then we have given life to both the killer and the one killed. They have expressed this meaning by saying: "Killing is the surest deterrent to killing."

Almighty God says, describing the horror of Hell:

﴿The Fire scorches their faces, and they therein are grim-faced.﴾

Al-lafh (scorching): the fire touches a thing with its heat and roasts it. Similar to it is al-nafh (blasting). ﴿And they therein are grim-faced.﴾ [al-Mu'minun]: the word "kalih" (grim-faced) is used even in colloquial speech: "So-and-so is kalih al-wajh," meaning his face has changed in a hideous way that is not pleasant to look at. They gave the image of a grim face as the head of a roasted sheep whose features the fire has altered, so that it becomes disfigured and grim, its upper lip stuck to its forehead and its lower lip to its chest, its teeth showing in a repulsive shape.

After that, the Truth, glorified is He, addresses them in an address that places the blame upon them and holds them responsible for what they have come to. Their Lord did not punish them at the outset; rather, He punished them after He had warned them and sent to them a Messenger bearing a clear path that explains the reward of the obedient and the punishment of the disobedient, and He alerted them to everything. Nevertheless, they disobeyed and denied, and they did not undertake any new action in accordance with what God had commanded. So then, they are the ones who fell short.

1 - Al-Zajjaj said: al-lafh and al-nafh have one meaning, except that al-nafh has a greater effect than it. Abu Mansur said: What supports his statement is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And if a breath of the punishment of your Lord should touch them...﴾ [al-Anbiya' 46]. [Lisan al-'Arab, entry: lafh]..

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 23, verse 105:

﴿Did not My verses used to be recited to you, and you used to deny them?﴾ (23:105):

Meaning: you are the cause of the punishment you are in. There is no argument for people against Allah after the messengers, and no one has an excuse after the delivery of the message. Therefore, when the people of the Fire enter the Fire, their Lord addresses them: ﴿Did there not come to you messengers from among you, reciting to you the verses of your Lord...﴾ (39:71).

The verse establishes that they are the wrongdoers before their own selves: ﴿And We did not wrong them, but they were wronging themselves﴾ (16:118). We did not surprise them with a punishment for something of which we had not made them aware; rather, We sent to them a messenger who commands them, forbids them, gives them glad tidings, and warns them.

Warning of evil before it occurs is itself a blessing among the blessings, as we said in Surah al-Rahman concerning His saying, the Exalted: ﴿There will be sent upon you both a flame of fire and smoke, and you will not be victorious. So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ (55:35-36). And is the Fire and the flame a blessing? Yes, it is a blessing, because We warn them of it before it befalls them, and you are still in the spaciousness of the world, and before you is the opportunity of making amends.

And the verses (āyāt), as we have said, are applied to the cosmic signs that draw people's attention to the existence of the Supreme Creator who originated this universe with this wondrous design; they are also applied to the miracles that establish the truthfulness of the Messenger in conveying from Allah; and they are applied to the verses bearing the rulings, which are the verses of the Qur'an.

We have brought you all of these verses, recited to you, and you hear them and see them, yet you denied. The meaning of ﴿recited to you﴾ (23:105) is that We alerted you to them and drew your attention to contemplating them, so that you cannot say: "We were heedless of them."

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 23, verse 106:

﴿Our Lord, our wretchedness overcame us, and we were a people astray.﴾ (23:106):

﴿Shiqwatuna.. (23:106)﴾ [Al-Mu'minun]: That is, al-shaqawa (wretchedness), which is the pain that possesses all the faculties of the self, leaving no aspect of it untouched. They say: "So-and-so is shaqi," meaning he is constricted and afflicted in every matter of his life, finding no ease in any of them.

It is as if, by their saying ﴿Our wretchedness overcame us..(23:106)﴾ [Al-Mu'minun], they wish to put the matter away from themselves and cast it upon Allah, the Exalted. They say: "O Lord, You have decreed wretchedness upon us from eternity, so there is no fault on us. And how could we make ourselves happy?" They say: "If our Lord had willed, we would not have done that."

And we say to them: Allah has decreed upon you from eternity, because He, glory be to Him, knew that you would choose this.

1 - Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir (6/4687): "The reading of the people of Madina, Abu 'Amr and 'Asim is 'shaqawatuna' (shiqwatuna), while the Kufans, except 'Asim, read 'shaqawatuna'."

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 23, verse 107:

﴿Our Lord, bring us out of it, and if we return, then indeed we are wrongdoers.﴾ (23:107)

So they described themselves as wrongdoers, just as He, glory be to Him, said of them in another verse: ﴿And if they were returned, they would indeed return to what they were forbidden, and indeed they are liars.﴾ (6:28)

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 23, verse 108:

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿He will say: "Be silent in it, and do not speak to Me."﴾

﴿Ukhsa'u (Be silent with abasement)﴾ [al-Mu'minun]: an eloquent word of rebuke, meaning: silence together with humiliation and disgrace. For this reason it is said to dogs. You may also say to your companion, "Be quiet" (uskut), as a form of honouring him, as when he speaks to you of his favour over you and of what you did for him, so you say to him, "Be quiet, be quiet," wishing him dignity and that he not stand before you in a position of weakness and abasement.

Among its meanings is that you become too weak to bear a thing, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then return the gaze twice; your gaze will return to you humbled (khasi'an) and weary (hasir)﴾ [al-Mulk, 4]: meaning, weak in bearing the light.

And in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And you certainly knew those among you who transgressed in the matter of the Sabbath, so We said to them, "Be apes, despised (khasi'in)"﴾ [al-Baqarah, 65]: meaning, expelled and removed from the nobility and honour of humanity. For this reason we see apes with exposed private parts, and with movements that do not befit human dignity.

Therefore, the meaning is not that they became apes; rather, it is that they were made into the form of apes. For this reason we see them, even until now, not concerned with matters of modesty and the exposure of nakedness.

So the meaning of ﴿Be silent in it, and do not speak to Me﴾ [al-Mu'minun, 108] is: be silent in a silence of abasement and disgrace, and what you have done to the believers in My name is enough for you.

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿Indeed, there was a group of My servants who said, "Our Lord, we have believed, so forgive us and have mercy upon us, and You are the best of the merciful."﴾

What is meant here is the weak among the believers, such as ʿAmmar, Bilal and Khabbab ibn al-Aratt,(1) and they used to say these words. They are good words that are not rejected; rather, they must be listened to, followed, and taken as an example.

1 - Mujahid said this, as transmitted from him by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir (6/4688).

**Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 23, verse 110:**

﴿Then you took them in mockery, until they made you forget My remembrance, and you used to laugh at them.﴾

We have spoken about this matter in His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿Indeed, those who committed crime used to laugh at those who believed. And when they passed by them, they would exchange winks. And when they returned to their people, they returned jesting. And when they saw them, they said, "Indeed, these are misguided." But they had not been sent as guardians over them. So today, those who believed will laugh at the disbelievers, upon couches, looking on. Have the disbelievers been rewarded for what they used to do?﴾ [al-Mutaffifin]

So: the disbelievers took the weak among the believers as objects of ridicule and mockery, and they went to extremes in this, until mockery and derision became their only occupation, and until mockery and derision preoccupied them from reflection and contemplation, so that no mental capacity remained in them to consider what these people believed in. This is the meaning of ﴿until they made you forget My remembrance…﴾ (110) [al-Mu'minun]: that is, mockery of the believers preoccupied you from belief in the One who created you and them.

Would that the matter had stopped at this degree of mockery! Rather, it went further, to the point that they laughed at the people of faith and made their own folk laugh: ﴿and you used to laugh at them﴾ (110) [al-Mu'minun]. In the other verse: ﴿And when they returned to their people, they returned jesting﴾ (31) [al-Mutaffifin]. The mockery of the people of falsehood toward the people of truth exists in every age, and even now we see those who mock the people of uprightness, religiosity and piety, and make fun of them.

1 – *Fakihin* (jesting): that is, they backbite people, speak about them, and make fun of them. *Al-fakih* is one who tells his companions stories and makes them laugh. [Lisan al-'Arab, root: f-k-h]

Then Allah, glorified is He, says:

﴿Indeed, I have rewarded them today for their patience; indeed, it is they who are the triumphant.﴾ (23:111)

When the people of faith patiently endured mockery and ridicule, Allah compensated them with honor and bliss. This is a matter that the believer must not overlook when his enemies mock him. He should remember the bounty of his Lord and the reward of his patience. Even if the one who mocks you is a servant who has limited power, your Lord, who honors you, has power without limits. You may then compare the hardship of patience under their harm with the sweetness of the bliss you find afterward as the reward of your patience.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 23, verse 112:

﴿He will say: "How many years did you remain on the earth?" (112)﴾:

Labitha (لبث): to stay and dwell. The meaning is: what is the number of years you spent on the earth? But why this question?

They said: Because what occupied you from a religion that guarantees you an everlasting appointment and an abiding bliss is the worldly life, which diverted you with its adornment, its embellishment and its desires. And even supposing you enjoyed this in the world, can it be compared with what has been prepared for the believers in the Hereafter of lasting bliss, which neither escapes them nor do they escape it?

When the Resurrection arrives, it will fall upon people who died just at its moment, so their stay will be brief, and upon people who died since the days of Adam, so their stay will be long. Thus, staying on the earth is, as they say, subject to gradation (maqul bil-tashkik). But do the dead perceive the period they stayed on the earth? It is known that they do not perceive time, because the perception of time comes through witnessing events, and the dead person does not feel time, since he does not experience events, just as the sleeper does not know the duration of his sleep. Everyone who was asked this question said: ﴿A day or part of a day...﴾ (259) [al-Baqarah].

This was said by ʿUzayr (ʿUzair), whom God caused to die for a hundred years and then raised up, and it was said by the People of the Cave (Ashab al-Kahf), whom God put to sleep for three hundred years and nine more, because this is the longest period a human can imagine for his sleep, and the sleeper cannot determine that precisely, because time is the child of event: if the event is absent, time is absent.

Therefore, the Exalted says of those who died, even from the days of Adam (peace be upon him): ﴿As if they had not remained but an evening or its morning (46)﴾ [al-Nazi'at].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 23, verse 113:

And in the same way, these people also say in answer to this question:

﴿They said, "We stayed a day or part of a day, so ask those who keep count."﴾

That is: the people of counting, those who are able to count and calculate, because we were not conscious enough to count how long we stayed. And what is meant by "those who keep count" (al-'adin) is the angels who count the days and reckon them.(1)

1 - Al-Qurtubi mentioned in his tafsir (6/4690), regarding the meaning of (al-'adin), two opinions:
- The reckoners, who know that. Said by Qatada.
- The angels who were with us in the world. Said by Mujahid.

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿He said, "You stayed only a little, if only you had known."﴾

"Inna" here means "ma" (not), i.e., "you stayed only a little." Whatever length of life you reckon, even if someone had died since the days of Adam (ﷺ)... [note: the honorific here is "عليه السلام", rendered as "peace be upon him"]

Correction to the above: rendering the passage faithfully:

"Inna" here means "ma" (negative particle, "not"), meaning: "you stayed only a little." Whatever length of life you reckon, even if counted from the days of Adam (peace be upon him), it will be little in comparison with the time that awaits you in the recompense of the Hereafter. What you remained in this world cannot be measured against the punishment of the Hereafter, which is extended and everlasting. This is ﴿if only you had known﴾ [al-Mu'minun]: you would know the length of the everlasting, enduring punishment to which you are going.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 23, verse 115:

﴿Did you then think that We had created you in vain, and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ (23:115)

(Hasiba) means "to think, to suppose": that is, what did you think about Our creating you? As He says in another place: ﴿Do people think that they will be left to say, "We believe," and that they will not be tested?﴾ (29:2). The word ﴿in vain﴾ ('abathan) means: 'abath is an action that has no purpose and no benefit from it, as you say: "What are you wasting your time on?" to someone who does an action that yields no benefit. Opposite to 'abath we say jadd (seriousness), and we say la'ib (play) and lahw (diversion); all of these are activities in the movements of life. But jadd is that you do a deed for a determined aim.

As for la'ib (play), it is that you do a deed which, in reality, has no aim at present except training yourself in movement and occupying your faculties, so that you do not turn to the corruption or harm of anything, as you buy your child a toy to play with, and he becomes occupied with it away from the valuable things in the house, which, if he played with them, he would break. So you direct his movements towards something to keep him from harmful things, or you teach him through play something that will benefit him later, such as swimming or horse riding.

Lahw (diversion) is like la'ib in that it has an aim which may come later, or an aim which negates harm, except that la'ib, when you practise it, does not distract you from something required, whereas lahw is that which distracts you from something required. For example, a child under seven plays at prayer times, so his action is called la'ib; but if he is ten, his action is called lahw, because it distracts him from the prayer, which is obligatory upon him.

Play trains you in things you may need at the time of seriousness, so they will be easy for you, whereas 'abath has no benefit in it. Therefore He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿Did you then think that We had created you in vain?﴾ (23:115). He negated that creation should be in vain without an aim, because God Most High created creation for a determined aim, and He set for them a method that defines this aim, and none sets a method for creation except the Creator.

As we said earlier: the craftsman who made this microphone did not make it and then ask us to search for a task for it; rather, before he made it he determined its task and its purpose, which is to carry sound over long distances. So, the aim is determined at the beginning and before the work.

He who determines the aim is the creative maker of the thing, and he is also the one who determines the soundness of the craft for its aim, and determines the law of its maintenance so that it performs its task in the best manner. And you, O human, are God's craftsmanship, so let Him determine for you your aim, and set for you the method of your life and the law of your maintenance: do this and do not do that.

So, the corruption of the world comes from the craft wanting to take the right of the craftsman in determining the aim, and in determining the method and the law of maintenance, and that is not its task. The Creator, when He determines for you the aim, sets for you the method that helps you toward your aim. But as for you: when are you able to perceive things so as to set an aim or set a law of maintenance?

You cannot reach this level before the age of twenty at best. So who, then, sets for you your aim and your law of maintenance before this age? None but your Creator, mighty and majestic. The situation will not be right unless we leave the craft to the Craftsman for aim, method and maintenance.

How can you think that God Most High created you in vain, when He is the One who summoned you into existence, prepared for you the foundations of your life and its necessities, and urged you, by employing your mind upon these foundations, to be able to enjoy, by the energy and power created by God Most High, so as to make your soul happy and make your life comfortable?

In the past we sat by the light of the oil lamp, and now by the lights of neon and crystal. However much your life becomes luxurious and the means of comfort are available to you, do not forget that they are a gift from God in matter, in energy and in the thinking mind; all of them are created by God, mighty and majestic, and you own none of them. The proof: if God takes away your reason, you become insane; and if He takes away your energy and power, you become weak, unable even to breathe. These are blessings bestowed upon you, not something inherent in you.

So, you must reflect upon your Creator, mighty and majestic, and what He has bestowed upon you of the foundations of life, so that you know that this creation cannot be in vain, and that it must have an aim which the Creator, glory be to Him, has drawn. And you, in yourself, try to set for yourself an aim in some particular part of the great aim for which God created you.

Do you not see the young child, how you care for him, teach him, and spend on him stage after stage, until he reaches the university, and you cling to a great hope that this child of yours will have a standing in society and a rank among people? This process in itself is an aim; but once he obtains the prestigious post, standing and rank, the matter ends with death.

So there must be another aim greater than this, an aim which extinction does not reach and which has no beyond. This great aim is meeting God and encountering the recompense, either to Paradise or to Hell.

We must take all matters of life and its particulars in the light of this truth: that we were not created in vain, but for an aim willed by God, and for it there are means by which it is reached.

Then He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ (23:115). (Turji'un, "you are returned") means: against your will, and without your choice, as though something were driving them, as in His words: ﴿On the Day they will be pushed toward the Fire of Hell with a violent push﴾ (52:13). That is: they will be thrust into it, struck on their necks, and driven like beasts.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 23, verse 116:

﴿So exalted is Allah, the True King; there is no deity except Him, Lord of the Noble Throne.﴾ (116)

﴿Fa-ta'ala…﴾ [al-Mu'minun]: He is far removed from imperfection and sanctified. The word "al-'uluw" (exaltation) means elevation in rank. We say: "So-and-so rose above so-and-so" (ʿalā fulān ʿalā fulān). But when we say "ta'ala Allah," the meaning is the highest exaltation. If He bestows some elevation upon others, it is a lower and changeable elevation, as evidenced by the fact that He exalts you and, if He wills, strips you of it. Thus, elevation is not inherent in you.

The word "al-mulk" (kingship) we know from one who owns a piece of land with what is on it, governs it, and has subjects. From the same root comes "al-malik" (the owner). It applies to any owner of anything, even if he has nothing but the garment he wears. But "al-Malik" (the King) is the one who owns those who own. He has dominion over the owners, and this kingship was not taken by His essence; rather, it was given to Him by God.

Therefore, God says: ﴿Say: O Allah, Possessor of sovereignty, You give sovereignty to whom You will and remove sovereignty from whom You will. You honor whom You will and You degrade whom You will.﴾ (26) [Al 'Imran]. For if the kingship of these kings were inherent, it would not have been removed from them. Do you not see that a worldly king grows strong, his affair becomes settled, he has a scepter, force, and violence, and so on? Yet despite all this, he cannot retain his kingdom. In a moment that kingdom collapses, even at the hand of one of his own soldiers. Indeed, perhaps his own country rejects him and will not even accept that he be buried in it, while some other states volunteer and agree to shelter his remains in their land. So what kind of kingship is this?

This is a sign that we see in every age, as though it were established, evidence of the truth of the verse: ﴿Say: O Allah, Possessor of sovereignty, You give sovereignty to whom You will and remove sovereignty from whom You will. You honor whom You will and You degrade whom You will.﴾ (26) [Al 'Imran]. So, if you have been given kingship by Allah, know that it is a gifted kingship. Whatever is settled for you, you cannot guarantee its continuance, because Allah has given you kingship for a purpose, and none possesses the purpose except Him, glorified is He.

Therefore, the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, is ﴿al-Malik al-Haqq﴾ (116) [al-Mu'minun]: meaning, the one whom no one can dislodge from His kingship or strip of it. He disposes of His kingdom as He wills, and no one contends with Him over it. If He grants some of His own kingdom to anyone, the reins of that kingship remain in His hand, glorified is He: if He wills, He extends it, and if He wills, He strips and removes it. He alone is the True King; as for others, their kingship is given and can be taken away. Even if He makes people kings, when people who ruled in the world come on the Day of Resurrection, He will say: ﴿Whose is the kingdom today?﴾ (16) [Ghafir].

You will notice that the phrase ﴿You give sovereignty﴾ (26) [Al 'Imran] is easy, in contrast to ﴿You remove sovereignty﴾ (26) [Al 'Imran], for in removal there is evidence of hardship and struggle, since the owner of kingship tries to hold onto it, cling to it, and contend for it. But can one contend with Allah?

So His saying, glorified is He: ﴿So exalted is Allah, the True King﴾ (116) [al-Mu'minun] means: He is far above creating you in vain, far above your fleeing from His grip, or your going out of His authority, or your being independent of His control in your creation, and far above your escaping or refusing His punishment, for there is no deity other than Him: ﴿there is no deity except Him, Lord of the Noble Throne﴾ (116) [al-Mu'minun].

The Truth, blessed and exalted is He, governs within the framework of: ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One (1). Allah, the Eternal Refuge (2). He neither begets nor is born (3). Nor is there to Him any equivalent (4).﴾ [al-Ikhlas]. So if He tells you something, know that there is no deity other than Him to oppose it.

"Al-'Arsh" (the Throne) is a symbol of the settling of an affair for the owner, because he is occupied with managing his kingdom, subduing those who oppose him, and disciplining his enemies. When that is settled for him, he sits upon his throne. Thus, sitting upon the throne means the stabilizing of affairs and the settling of the matter of kingship. Therefore, after creating creation, the Truth, glorified is He, "istawa 'ala al-'Arsh" (established Himself upon the Throne).

The Throne also indicates control and authority. The Throne of Allah is a noble throne, because His exaltation over you is not to humiliate and demean you, but He is exalted over you so as to elevate you toward Himself and give you of His bounty. As we have said before, it is in our interest that Allah be the Majestic, and it is part of the greatness of the Truth, glorified is He, that greatness belongs to Him, so that when everyone knows that greatness belongs to Allah alone, no one is arrogant toward anyone.

The Truth, glorified is He, says: ﴿And to Him belongs greatness in the heavens and the earth, and He is the Mighty, the Wise﴾ (37) [al-Jathiyah].

Therefore, they say in proverbs: (Whoever has no great one buys himself a great one), meaning: so that he may live in his shadow. So the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, exalts Himself for the benefit of His creation.

And from this is what we said regarding the matter of servitude: that it is hateful and burdensome if it is to human beings, because the master takes the best of his servant, whereas it is beloved if it is to Allah, the Exalted, because in servitude to Allah the servant receives the best of his Lord.

If the thrones of this world are for control and domination over people's destinies, the draining of their blood, and the taking of their goods, then your Lord's throne is a noble throne, and "the noble" in everything is the highest of its ends. Read His saying, exalted is He: ﴿How many gardens and springs they left behind (25), and crops and a noble station (26)﴾ [al-Dukhan].

And when He enjoins us regarding parents, He says, glorified is He: ﴿And do not say to them "uff," nor repel them, but speak to them a noble word (23)﴾ [al-Isra'].

Thus the Noble Throne is the highest end of kingship, because kingship is not domination and coercion; rather, it is kingship for the benefit of people. The Truth, blessed and exalted is He, when He created life, distributed the causes of bounty within it, but He made in it the strong and capable, and He made in it the weak and incapable. Then He commanded the strong to take the hand of the weak and to support him. Generosity is the extension of the strong's benefit to the weak, so every virtuous trait is described as generosity (karam).

So beware of understanding that your Lord's throne is for domination, haughtiness, and tyranny, for it is a noble throne.

Then the Truthful (al-Haqq), glory be to Him, says:

﴿And whoever calls upon another god along with Allah, for which he has no proof, then his account is only with his Lord. Indeed, the disbelievers will not succeed.﴾ (23:117):

﴿Calls upon along with Allah...﴾ (23:117) [al-Mu'minun]: i.e., worships along with Allah. Worship (ʿibadah) is obedience to the one worshipped in His commands and prohibitions. But how can you call upon a god that neither benefits you nor harms you, and for whose divinity you have no proof? Therefore He threatens and warns him, saying: ﴿then his account is only with his Lord...﴾ (23:117) [al-Mu'minun]: i.e., his Lord, the Truth. ﴿Indeed, the disbelievers will not succeed﴾ (23:117) [al-Mu'minun].

It is remarkable that the surah begins with His saying: ﴿The believers have certainly succeeded﴾ (23:1) [al-Mu'minun], and ends with His saying: ﴿Indeed, the disbelievers will not succeed﴾ (23:117) [al-Mu'minun]: i.e., the opposite of what it began with. You should reflect on what lies between these two brackets. Since the matter is one of faith, whose people succeed, and disbelief, whose people do not succeed, then hold fast to your Lord and adhere to His method in "do" (ifʿal) and "do not do" (lā tafʿal).

And say, "My Lord, forgive and have mercy, and You are the best of the merciful" (23:118).

If the self overcomes you in some matter of sins, then remember this: if you commit a lapse, beware lest you forget this truth, and turn to your Lord, for He is Oft-Forgiving (ghaffar). He has prescribed repentance (tawbah) for you so that you may repent, and seeking forgiveness (istighfar) so that you may seek it. He, glory be to Him, is more merciful to you than a mother is to her child, and He is the best of the merciful.

The meaning of "Forgive me..." (23:118): that is, the sins that have passed before. "...and have mercy..." (23:118): that is, have mercy on us, so that we do not fall into sins in the future, and protect us from slips in the future course of our lives. So: hold fast to your Lord and to the method (manhaj) of your Lord in every state; let nothing turn you away from it.
